абсолютно.etymology: Adverb formed from абсолютный ('absolute, complete'), borrowed via German absolut or French absolu from Latin absolūtus ('freed, unrestricted, complete, unconditional'), the past participle of absolvere ('to loosen from, set free, complete').

аванс.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century from French avance ('advance payment; lead, step forward'), deverbal noun from avancer ('to move forward, advance'), from Vulgar Latin *abantiāre (from Late Latin abante 'in front, before', whence French avant).

history.meaning: in front → to advance → advance payment
advance payment (on wages or a contract)

адвокат.etymology: Borrowed under Peter the Great (early 18th century) via German Advokat and Polish adwokat from Latin advocātus ('one called to aid a party in court, legal witness or counsel'), past participle of advocāre ('to summon, call to one's aid', from ad- 'to' + vocāre 'to call', from vōx 'voice').

history.meaning: to call to one's aid → legal counsel

ай.etymology: Primary expressive interjection of sudden pain, fright, or surprise, inherited from Proto-Slavic *aj (and paralleled across Indo-European and other languages, compare German ei, French aïe, Sanskrit ē).

айфон.etymology: Borrowed in 2007 from English iPhone, the smartphone brand introduced by Apple Inc., coined from the prefix i- (originally standing for 'internet, individual, instruct, inform, inspire' in the 1998 iMac) + phone (short for telephone, from Ancient Greek φωνή 'voice, sound').

акварель.etymology: Borrowed from French aquarelle, from Italian acquerella ('watercolour'), a diminutive built on acqua 'water', from Latin aqua.
акварель.notes: In Russian акварель names both the paint medium (писать акварелью 'to paint in watercolour') and a finished watercolour picture.

акклиматизация.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French acclimatation / German Akklimatisation ('adaptation to a new climate or environment'), formed from the Latin prefix ad- ('to') + French climat ('climate', from Ancient Greek κλίμα klíma 'inclination of the earth toward the sun, latitude, climate') + -isation / -ация.

аккорд.etymology: Borrowed from French accord (and Italian accordo), from Vulgar Latin *accordare 'to bring into harmony, tune together', built on Latin ad- 'to' + cor 'heart'.

алкоголь.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Alkohol or French alcool from Medieval Latin alcohol, originally borrowed from Arabic الْكُحْل (al-kuḥl, 'finely powdered antimony/kohl eye cosmetic obtained by sublimation'). Renaissance alchemists (notably Paracelsus) extended alcohol from 'any fine sublimated powder' to 'distilled spirit of wine' (alcohol vini).

history.meaning: sublimated essence → distilled spirit of wine

аллергия.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from German Allergie, coined in 1906 by the Viennese pediatrician Clemens von Pirquet from Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, 'other, different') + ἔργον (érgon, 'work, reaction'), literally 'altered reactivity' of the immune system.

апельсин.etymology: Borrowed from Dutch appelsien, itself modelled on French pomme de Sine, literally 'apple from China', reflecting the sweet orange's trade route from East Asia to northern Europe.
апельсин.notes: Compare персик ('peach', originally 'Persian fruit') for another Russian fruit name preserving an old geographic origin.

арест.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via German Arrest and Polish areszt from Medieval Latin arrestum ('seizure, detention by order of a court'), from Vulgar Latin *arrestāre ('to cause to stop, detain', from ad- 'to' + restāre 'to remain, stand back', whence also French arrêt).

арестовать.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via Polish aresztować and German arretieren / arrestieren from Medieval Latin arrestāre ('to stop, detain by legal authority'), formed in Russian with the verbal suffix -овать on арест ('arrest').

архив.etymology: Borrowed under Peter the Great (early 18th century, originally feminine архива) via German Archiv and French archives from Late Latin archīum / archīvum ('public records office'), from Ancient Greek ἀρχεῖον (arkheîon, 'town hall, magistrate's residence where public records were kept'), derived from ἀρχή (arkhḗ, 'beginning, rule, magistracy').

балкон.etymology: Borrowed via French balcon from Italian balcone 'balcony, gallery', built on a Germanic word for a wooden beam or scaffold (*balko, akin to English balk and Russian балка 'beam').

банк.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via German Bank (or French banque) from Italian banca / banco ('moneychanger's bench or counter table'), itself an early borrowing from Lombardic/Germanic *banki ('bench'). When a medieval Italian banker failed, his bench was broken (banca rotta, whence банкрот 'bankrupt').

history.meaning: moneychanger's table or bench → financial bank
bank (financial institution; pot in card games)

rootFamily.gloss: banquet (from the same Italian root banco 'bench')

банкет.etymology: Borrowed in the late 17th or early 18th century via German Bankett (and Polish bankiet) from French banquet ('feast, ceremonial dinner'), itself borrowed from Italian banchetto, a diminutive of banco ('bench, table'), originally referring to a light meal or snack eaten on a bench before coming to mean a grand formal dinner.

rootFamily.gloss: bank (from the same Italian root banco 'bench')

бар.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from English bar ('counter across which drinks are served; pub, drinking establishment'), which comes from Old French barre ('barrier, rod, counter separating the server from patrons').

бармен.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English barman ('bartender'), a compound of bar ('tavern counter') and man.

барный.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ный from бар ('bar, pub; drinks counter', borrowed from English bar).

history.meaning: bar → of a bar (e.g. барная стойка 'bar counter')

башня.etymology: Developed from Old East Slavic башта, borrowed via Polish baszta or Czech bašta from Italian bastia 'fortified tower, bastion'. In Russian the ending was reshaped with the native place suffix -ня (as in пашня, таможня).

cognates.meaning: fortified projection (from the same Italian family)

башня.notes: Notice the fleeting vowel in the genitive plural: одна башня -> много башен.

беременный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic беремяньныи ('pregnant', literally 'carrying a burden'), displaying East Slavic pleophony -ере- (compare Old Church Slavonic брѣменьнъ), derived from беремя ('load, burden, armful', standard Russian бремя 'burden'), from Proto-Slavic *bermę ('load, that which is borne'), from the PIE root *bʰer- ('to carry, bear'; cognate with English bear and birth).

history.meaning: burden, load → carrying a child, pregnant

rootFamily.gloss: to take (from the same PIE root *bʰer-)

беспорядок.etymology: Formed in Russian with the privative prefix без- / бес- ('without, lack of') and порядок ('order, sequence, tidy arrangement', derived from по- + ряд 'row, line, order', Proto-Slavic *rędъ).

history.meaning: lack of order, disorder, mess; (pl.) riots/disturbances

близкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic близькыи (extended with the adjectival suffix -к- from older близъ 'near'), from Proto-Slavic *blizъ / *blizъkъ ('near, close').

блин.etymology: Altered in Old East Slavic блинъ from earlier млинъ (with dissimilation of м-н > б-н; compare Ukrainian млинець), from Proto-Slavic *mlinъ ('pancake, flat cake made of ground flour'), derived from the root of молоть ('to grind grain in a mill', Proto-Slavic *melti, PIE *melh₂-). In modern colloquial Russian, блин! is also widely used as a minced oath ('damn! shoot!') substituting for a taboo profanity sharing the initial бл-.

history.meaning: to grind → batter cake made of ground meal

богатый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic богатыи (and Old Church Slavonic богатъ), from Proto-Slavic *bogatъ ('rich, wealthy, endowed by fortune'), formed with the suffix *-atъ from the archaic noun sense of *bogъ ('share, portion, wealth, good fortune', cognate with Sanskrit bhága- 'fortune, wealth, dispenser/lord' and Avestan baγa-; the same word that gave Бог 'God', originally 'giver of good fortune/shares').

бокал.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French bocal or Italian boccale ('jug, goblet, drinking glass') from Late Latin baucālis, itself from Ancient Greek βαύκαλις (baúkalis, 'vessel for cooling wine or water').

болтать.etymology: Inherited East Slavic expressive/onomatopoeic verb (compare Ukrainian бовтати 'to stir, splash, chatter'), originally meaning 'to shake, stir, slosh liquid back and forth' (as in болтать ногами 'to dangle/swing one's legs' or болтунья 'scrambled eggs'). By metaphor ('wagging one's tongue'), болтать языком became the standard colloquial verb for 'to chatter, chat, blab'.

history.meaning: to stir, splash, swing back and forth
to swing, stir; to chat, chatter idly

больница.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic больница ('infirmary, hospital, house for the sick', attested in monastery rules from the 11th century), formed from больной ('sick, ill', from боль 'pain, illness') + the place/institution suffix -ница.

больно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate formed from the neuter short form of больной ('painful, sore, sick'), derived from боль ('pain, ache'), from Proto-Slavic *bolь ('pain, sickness').

брат.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic братъ (older братръ), from Proto-Slavic *bratrъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr ('brother') — one of the most stable kinship words across Indo-European languages, cognate with English brother, Latin frāter, and Sanskrit bhrātṛ.
брат.notes: Notice the irregular collective-origin plural: **братья**, genitive **братьев**.

бросить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бросити, from Proto-Slavic *brositi ('to scrape off, strip, fling, throw'). Originally referring to stripping flax or scraping off bark/buds, in Russian it became the general perfective verb for 'to throw, fling' and figuratively 'to abandon, quit, leave someone'.

history.meaning: to throw; to quit; to leave/dump (someone)

буддийский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ский from буддизм / Будда ('Buddha'), borrowed from Sanskrit बुद्ध (Buddha, literally 'the Awakened One, the Enlightened One', past participle of budh- 'to awake, perceive, understand', cognate with Russian будить 'to wake up').

будущий.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бѫдѫщии ('that which will be, future'), the active participle formed from the future stem бѫд- / буд- ('will be', 1st sg. буду) of быти / быть ('to be', Proto-Slavic *bǫdǫ from PIE *bʰuH- with nasal infix).

history.meaning: future, next (and neuter noun будущее 'the future')

букет.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French bouquet ('nosegay, bunch of flowers; aroma of wine'), originally a Norman-Picard dialectal diminutive of Old French bosc / bois ('wood, grove, little clump of trees').

history.meaning: little wood, clump of foliage → bunch of flowers; wine aroma

букинист.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French bouquiniste 'dealer in second-hand and antiquarian books', from bouquin 'old book', itself taken from Middle Dutch boeckin ('little book').
букинист.notes: Букинистический магазин is the standard Russian name for a second-hand or antiquarian bookshop.

бульон.etymology: Borrowed from French bouillon 'broth', from bouillir 'to boil', which goes back to Latin bullire 'to bubble, boil' from bulla 'bubble'.
бульон.notes: Note how Russian spells the palatal French -ill- with льйо -> льо: бульон.

бумага.etymology: Recorded in Old Russian from the 14th century, first meaning 'cotton wool' (still seen in хлопчатобумажный 'cotton') and then 'rag paper'. Vasmer considers borrowing from Italian bambagia ('cotton', from Medieval Greek βάμβαξ, ultimately Persian pambak) the likeliest route.

бумажник.etymology: Formed in Russian from бумага ('paper; paper banknote') + the noun suffix -ник: originally a pocket case for carrying folded paper notes and documents, hence 'wallet'.

history.meaning: pocket wallet for notes and papers

morphemes.meaning: paper (from бумага with г -> ж alternation)

бутерброд.etymology: Borrowed from German Butterbrot, 'bread and butter', a compound of Butter 'butter' and Brot 'bread'. In Russian the word widened to any open sandwich, so a бутерброд can carry cheese or sausage and no butter at all.
бутерброд.notes: A sandwich made of two slices is often called сэндвич; бутерброд is usually open.

буханка.etymology: Formed with -ка from dialectal бухон 'round loaf', borrowed via Polish bochen 'loaf of bread' and Old High German fohhenza, ultimately going back to Latin focacium 'hearth-baked bread' (from focus 'hearth', the same Latin source as Italian focaccia).

бывший.etymology: Lexicalized past active participle of быть ('to be', Old East Slavic быти, Proto-Slavic *byti, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- 'to become, grow, be'). From its literal participial sense 'having been', it became the standard adjective for 'former, ex-'.

быть.etymology: Быть is an inherited Slavic verb. Vasmer compares Lithuanian būti and older Indo-European words for being, becoming and coming into existence. That older family helps explain why the history of this everyday verb reaches beyond the modern English gloss to be.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: быть

вальс.etymology: Borrowed from French valse, which in turn comes from German Walzer, a noun from walzen 'to turn, to roll'. The dance is named for its turning steps.

вариант.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via German Variante or French variante from Latin variāns (genitive variantis, 'varying, differing'), present participle of variāre ('to vary, change, diversify'), from varius ('varied, diverse').

великий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic великыи (and Old Church Slavonic великъ, extended with -ик- from older вель / велии 'great'), from Proto-Slavic *velikъ ('great, large').
великий.notes: In modern Russian, the long form **великий** means 'great, eminent' (Пётр Великий), whereas the short form **велик / велика / велики** means 'too big (in clothing/shoe size)' (*костюм мне велик*).

великолепный.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic великолѣпьнъ ('magnificently fitting, majestic, splendid'), a calque of Ancient Greek μεγαλοπρεπής (megaloprepḗs, 'befitting a great person, magnificent'), compounded from великъ ('great') + лѣпъ ('fitting, comely, beautiful', from Proto-Slavic *lěpъ, preserved in нелепый 'absurd, unfitting' and Ukrainian ліпий / гарний).

вентилятор.etymology: Borrowed via German Ventilator from Latin ventilator 'winnower, airer', an agent noun from ventilare 'to fan, wave in the air', itself built on ventus 'wind'.

верить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣрити ('to believe, trust'), a denominative verb formed from вѣра ('faith, belief, trust'), from Proto-Slavic *věra (related to Latin vērus 'true' and German wahr 'true', from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁ro-).

верный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣрьныи (and Old Church Slavonic вѣрьнъ 'faithful, true, trustworthy'), formed with the suffix -ный from вѣра ('faith, trust, truth'), from Proto-Slavic *věra (cognate with Latin vērus 'true' and German wahr 'true').

весёлый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic веселыи (and Old Church Slavonic веселъ 'merry, joyful, glad'), from Proto-Slavic *veselъ ('joyful, merry'), with close Baltic cognates (Latvian vesels 'healthy, whole, hale'). The semantic shift between 'healthy, hale, vigorous' (Baltic) and 'merry, cheerful' (Slavic) is an ancient Balto-Slavic development.

ветчина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ветъшина ('cured or aged meat, ham', attested in the 16th-century Domostroi), formed with the meat-designation suffix -ина (as in свинина, говядина, баранина) from ветхий ('old, aged', Old East Slavic ветъхъ, Proto-Slavic *vetъxъ 'old', cognate with Latin vetus 'old'), with dissimilation of -тш- > -тч-. Originally ветчина meant 'aged/cured salted pork' as opposed to fresh pork (свежина).

вечер.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вечеръ, from Proto-Slavic *večerъ, closely cognate with Lithuanian vãkaras and Latvian vakars ('evening'), and compared by Vasmer with Latin vesper and Ancient Greek ἕσπερος.

вечеринка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the compound suffix -инка (diminutive of dialectal/archaic вечерина 'evening gathering') from вечер ('evening', Old East Slavic вечеръ, Proto-Slavic *večerъ).

вечером.etymology: Lexicalized instrumental singular of вечер ('evening'), used adverbially to express time when ('in the evening'). Inherited from Old East Slavic вечеръ, from Proto-Slavic *večerъ (compare Lithuanian vãkaras 'evening').

взрослый.etymology: Formed from the past active participle or verbal adjective of взрасти / взросло ('to grow up'), built from the upward prefix вз- ('up') + рос- (the past-tense stem of расти 'to grow', from Proto-Slavic *orsti) + -лый. Functions both as an adjective ('adult, grown-up') and as a substantivized noun ('an adult').

взятка.etymology: Formed in Russian from взять ('to take', from Old East Slavic възяти, a compound of въз- + яти 'to take') with the noun suffix -ка. Originally meaning simply 'that which is taken, a levy, exaction, or trick in cards', it specialized in administrative and everyday usage to mean an illicit payment or 'bribe'.

взяточник.etymology: Formed in Russian with the agent suffix -ник from взятка ('bribe', with stem alternation к > ч before -ник), itself derived from взять ('to take', Old East Slavic възяти).

видео.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English video, which was coined in television technology in the 1930s (as a counterpart to audio) from Latin videō ('I see'), first-person singular present of vidēre ('to see', cognate with Russian видеть).

history.meaning: I see → television/visual signal and recording

вилла.etymology: Borrowed via Italian villa (or German Villa) from Latin vīlla ('country house, estate, farmstead'), related to vīcus ('village, group of houses').

вино.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вино (and Old Church Slavonic вино), borrowed in the Proto-Slavic period (*vino) via Gothic wein or directly from Latin vīnum ('wine'), an ancient Mediterranean wanderword shared with Ancient Greek οἶνος (oînos).

виски.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from English whisky / whiskey, itself an anglicization of Scottish Gaelic uisge-beatha and Irish uisce beatha ('water of life', a calque of Medieval Latin aqua vītae; compare the parallel formation of Russian водка from вода 'water').

власть.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic власть ('rule, dominion, authority, power'), corresponding to native East Slavic волость ('district, territory under a ruler', with pleophony -оло-), from Proto-Slavic *volstь, formed with the suffix *-tь from *volsti (1st sg. *voldǫ, 'to rule, govern', whence владеть; cognate with Gothic waldan and English wield).

влюбиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed with the prefix в- ('into') + любить ('to love', from Proto-Slavic *ľubiti) + -ся. Literally, 'to enter into a state of love, fall in love' (constructed with в + accusative: влюбиться в кого-то).

внимание.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вънимание ('heeding, listening closely, attention'), the verbal noun of вънимати / внимать ('to take in with the mind or ears, heed'), formed from вън- ('into', with epenthetic -н-) and имати ('to take', iterative of яти, Proto-Slavic *jьmati).

вовсе.etymology: Univerbated adverbial phrase formed from the preposition во ('in, into') and все / всё ('all, everything', from Proto-Slavic *vьxъ / *vьśь). Originally meaning 'in all respects, completely, altogether', in modern Russian it is most often used as an intensifier with negation: **вовсе не** / **вовсе нет** ('not at all, by no means').

вода.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вода, from Proto-Slavic *voda, continuing the ancient Proto-Indo-European root *wódr̥ ('water'), cognate with English water, German Wasser, Ancient Greek ὕδωρ, and Lithuanian vanduo.

водка.etymology: Formed as a diminutive of вода ('water', Old East Slavic вода, Proto-Slavic *voda) with the suffix -ка. First documented in Russian and Polish sources in the 15th–16th centuries for medicinal herbal tinctures and distilled spirits, paralleling Latin aqua vītae ('water of life') and Gaelic uisge beatha ('whisky').

history.meaning: little water → medicinal tincture, distilled grain spirit

возле.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic възлѣ ('beside, alongside'), univerbated from the preposition въз ('up along, by') + the locative/dative form лѣ (from the archaic Proto-Slavic root *lě- / *lěv- or *lьg-; Vasmer favors a formation parallel to подлѣ 'beside', remodelled on въз-).

война.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic воина ('war, military campaign'), from Proto-Slavic *vojьna, derived from *vojь ('warrior; army, host', preserved in воин 'warrior' and войско 'army'), from Proto-Indo-European *weyh₁- ('to pursue, hunt, strive after'; compare Lithuanian výti 'to chase' and Latin vis 'force').

волос.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic волосъ (showing East Slavic pleophony -оло-; compare Old Church Slavonic власъ and Polish włos), from Proto-Slavic *volsъ ('hair'), with close Indo-Iranian cognates (Avestan varəsa- 'hair of the head', Persian gurs).
волос.notes: Singular **волос** refers to a single strand of hair; hair on the head collectively is plural **волосы** (genitive plural **волос**).

вор.etymology: Attested in Russian from the late 16th century (originally meaning 'state criminal, traitor, rebel, impostor' — as in Тушинский вор for False Dmitry II — before narrowing in the 18th century to 'thief', displacing older тать). Usually connected by Vasmer to the same root as врать ('to lie, babble, deceive', with o-grade ablaut вор- < *vorъ 'deceiver, crook'), though Finno-Ugric connections have also been proposed.

воробей.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic воробии and Proto-Slavic *vorbьjь 'sparrow', widely traced by Vasmer and Slavic etymologists to an expressive sound-imitating root echoing the bird's quick chirping.
воробей.notes: Declines with soft -ь- throughout the oblique stem: воробей -> воробья, воробьи, воробьёв.

воровать.etymology: Denominative verb formed with the suffix -овать from вор ('thief, criminal', attested from the 16th century). While Old East Slavic stole was красти (modern красть / украсть), воровать became the everyday colloquial and general imperfective verb for 'to steal, pilfer, embezzle'.

history.meaning: rogue, rebel, thief → to commit crimes, steal

воск.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *voskъ 'wax', from a Balto-Slavic and Indo-European word for beeswax shared directly with Lithuanian vaskas and English wax.

восток.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic въстокъ ('sunrise, rising, east'), a loan-translation of Ancient Greek anatole ('rising of the sun; the east'), built on въз- ('up') + -токъ ('flowing, rising, course').
восток.notes: Used in the singular: на восток ('to the east'), на востоке ('in the east'), с востока ('from the east').

восторг.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въсторгъ ('ecstasy, rapture, being snatched up in spirit'), a deverbal noun from въсторгнѫти / восторгнуть ('to tear/snatch upward'), built from въз- ('up') + торг- ('to tear, pull, jerk', as in расторгнуть 'to tear up a contract' and тормошить). Originally a mystical religious term translating Greek ἔκστασις ('ecstasy, transport of the soul'), it became the everyday word for 'delight, enthusiasm, rapture'.

вот-вот.etymology: Reduplicated expressive adverb formed by doubling the demonstrative particle вот ('here is, look!'), expressing that an action is on the verge of happening ('any second now, just about to').

history.meaning: right now, any moment now, just about to

враг.etymology: Borrowed in its South Slavic / Old Church Slavonic form врагъ ('enemy, foe; the Devil'), alongside native East Slavic ворогъ (with pleophony -оро-), from Proto-Slavic *vorgъ ('enemy, outcast, persecutor'; compare Lithuanian var̃gas 'misery, distress' and Gothic wrikan 'to persecute', English wreak/wretch).

врать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьрати ('to babble, talk nonsense, lie'), from Proto-Slavic *vьrati ('to speak, chatter'). In older Russian up to the 18th century, врать often meant simply 'to chatter idly, babble'; Vasmer connects the root with Old Prussian īrist ('to say') and Ancient Greek εἴρω (eírō, 'to speak') and ῥήτωρ (rhḗtōr, 'orator', from PIE *werh₁- 'to speak', cognate with English word and Latin verbum), and compares врач ('physician', originally 'incantation speaker, healer').

history.meaning: to talk nonsense → to tell lies

врач.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic врачь ('physician, healer'), from Proto-Slavic *vračь, formed with the agent suffix *-čь from *vьrati ('to speak, recite charms', modern Russian врать). Originally врач denoted a traditional folk healer or medicine man who cured sickness by reciting incantations; in standard Russian врать shifted to 'to tell lies', while врач became the formal word for a medical doctor.

history.meaning: to speak charms → incantation healer, physician

врунишка.etymology: Affectionate or mildly deprecatory diminutive formed with the suffix -ишка from врун ('liar'), itself an agent noun built on врать ('to lie, tell fibs', from Old East Slavic вьрати, Proto-Slavic *vьrati).

history.meaning: to lie → liar → little liar, fibber

все.etymology: Plural form ('all, everyone') of the pronoun весь ('all, whole'), inherited from Old East Slavic вьсь (plural вьси), from Proto-Slavic *vьxъ / *vьśь ('all, whole'), cognate with Lithuanian visas ('all') and Sanskrit viśva- ('all, every').

встречаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive/reciprocal verb formed from встречать ('to meet'), derived from встретить ('to meet'), which goes back to Old East Slavic въстрѣтити (with epenthetic -т- inserted in the cluster -ср-), from Proto-Slavic *vъz- + *sъrětiti ('to encounter, come upon').

history.meaning: to meet, go out to greet
to meet each other; to date, go out

всё-таки.etymology: Compound concessive particle formed in Russian from всё ('all, still, nonetheless', neuter singular of весь 'all') and the emphatic particle таки ('after all, even so', derived from так 'thus, so', Proto-Slavic *tako).

history.meaning: all the same, after all, nevertheless

вчерашний.etymology: Temporal adjective formed with the suffix -шний (used to form adjectives from time/place adverbs, as in сегодняшний, домашний, здешний) from вчера ('yesterday'), which goes back to Old East Slavic вьчера, originally the genitive singular of вечеръ ('evening', Proto-Slavic *večerъ).

вы.etymology: Вы is an inherited Slavic second-person plural pronoun, already present in Old Russian and Old Church Slavonic. Vasmer relates it to forms such as Latin vos and discusses how older pronoun forms were remodelled within the Slavic case system. Addressing one person politely is a use of the plural pronoun, not its original basic meaning.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: вы

выборы.etymology: Plural of выбор ('choice, selection'), formed as a deverbal noun from выбирать / выбрать ('to choose, elect'), built from the prefix вы- ('out') and брать ('to take', from Proto-Slavic *bьrati). In the plural, выборы specialized in the political sense of 'elections'.

вывеска.etymology: Built natively from the verb вывесить 'to hang out' (вы- 'out' + весить 'to hang') + -ка: literally 'something hung outside' over a shop door to show its name or trade.

выгнать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix вы- ('out') and гнать ('to drive, chase'), inherited from Old East Slavic гънати, from Proto-Slavic *gъnati ('to drive cattle, chase', from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen- 'to strike, drive').

history.meaning: to drive out, kick out, expel

выгореть.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix вы- ('out, completely') and гореть ('to burn'), inherited from Old East Slavic горѣти and Proto-Slavic *gorěti. In colloquial Russian (especially in the negative: дело не выгорело 'the deal didn't pan out'), the figurative sense 'to succeed, come off' arose from metallurgy, brick-firing, or tar-distilling, where a batch had to burn through properly to yield a good result.

history.meaning: to burn out/down; (colloq.) to pan out, succeed

вызвать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix вы- ('out') and звать ('to call', Old East Slavic зъвати, Proto-Slavic *zъvati). Literally 'to call out', whence 'to summon (a doctor, taxi, or witness), challenge, or cause'.

history.meaning: to call out, summon; to cause

выиграть.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix вы- ('out, winning through action') and играть ('to play', from Old East Slavic играти, Proto-Slavic *jьgrati). Literally, 'to obtain or come out ahead by playing'.

history.meaning: to win (a game, prize, or election)

выключить.etymology: Coined in late 19th- / early 20th-century technical Russian as a semantic calque of German ausschalten ('to switch off, disconnect a circuit'), formed from вы- ('out') + ключить (built on ключ 'key, switch', from Proto-Slavic *kľučь 'hook, key, bolt'), as the antonym of включить ('to include; to switch on').

выполнять.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of выполнить ('to fulfill, carry out, perform'), formed from the prefix вы- ('out, completely') and полнить ('to fill', from полный 'full', Old East Slavic пълныи, Proto-Slavic *pъlnъ, cognate with English full). Literally, 'to fill out to completion, fulfill' (compare English fulfill from full).

выслушать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the exhaustive prefix вы- ('out, to the end') and слушать ('to listen', from Proto-Slavic *slušati). Means 'to listen to someone all the way through, hear someone out'.

history.meaning: to hear out, listen to the end

выставка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with the suffix -ка from выставить ('to set out, put on display, exhibit'), built from вы- ('out') + ставить ('to put, place upright', Proto-Slavic *staviti). Like Latin expositiō / English exhibition, it literally means 'a setting out on public view'.

history.meaning: setting out on display → exhibition, show, expo

выступать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of выступить ('to step forward, step out; to perform or speak in public'), formed from the prefix вы- ('out, forth') and ступать ('to step, tread', from Proto-Slavic *stǫpati). Literally, 'to step out in front of an audience or assembly'.

history.meaning: to step forward → to speak in public, perform on stage

rootFamily.gloss: to step on; to come (of time)

высший.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вꙑшьшии ('higher, highest, supreme'), the synthetic comparative/superlative degree of высокий ('high, tall', Proto-Slavic *vysokъ, comparative *vyšьjь).

вытереть.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix вы- ('out, clean, dry') and тереть ('to rub, wipe', 1st sg. тру), inherited from Old East Slavic терти and Proto-Slavic *terti ('to rub, grate, wipe', from PIE *terh₁- 'to rub, turn', cognate with Latin terō 'to rub, wear away' and Greek τείρω).

выходной.etymology: Adjective formed from выход ('exit, going out; day off from duty'), derived from выходить / выйти ('to go out, step out'). Substantivized from выходной день ('day when workers or servants are free to go out from work'), выходной (plural выходные 'weekend') became the standard noun for a day off.

history.meaning: going out → day off work; (pl.) weekend

гадость.etymology: Abstract and concrete noun formed with the suffix -ость from гадкий ('nasty, repulsive, vile') and гад ('reptile, creeping creature, vermin'), inherited from Old East Slavic гадъ and Proto-Slavic *gadъ ('reptile, snake, loathsome creature', originally an old taboo-avoidance word connected with disgust, cognate with Lithuanian gė́da 'shame, disgrace' and Old High German quāt 'filth, dung, evil').

history.meaning: nastiness, filth, vile thing or act

генерал.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-17th century via German General and Polish generał from French général (shortened from capitaine général, 'captain in overall command'), from Latin generālis ('general, pertaining to the whole class or army'), from genus ('kind, race, class').

history.meaning: general, overall → commander of the whole force

гирлянда.etymology: Borrowed from French guirlande ('garland, wreath'), from Italian ghirlanda, ultimately connected with words for twisting or braiding foliage and wire.

history.meaning: floral garland; string of festive lights

глазурь.etymology: Borrowed from German Glasur 'glaze (on pottery or pastry)', formed on Glas 'glass' because a glaze dries to a smooth, glass-like shine.
глазурь.notes: Covers both ceramic glaze and sweet culinary icing (лимонная глазурь, шоколадная глазурь).

глупо.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate formed from the neuter short form of глупый ('stupid, foolish'), from Proto-Slavic *glupъ ('foolish, dull, deafened').

глупость.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from глупый ('stupid, foolish', from Proto-Slavic *glupъ). Denotes both the quality of foolishness and a specific foolish act or remark ('nonsense, silly thing').

гном.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century via German Gnom / French gnome from New Latin gnomus ('subterranean earth-spirit, dwarf guarding underground treasures'), coined in the 16th century by the Swiss alchemist Paracelsus (probably from Ancient Greek γνώμη gnṓmē 'intelligence, thought' or γνοφός 'darkness', or modeled on genomos 'earth-dweller').

говорить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic говорити, from Proto-Slavic *govoriti, originally an expressive verb meaning 'to murmur, hubbub, talk noisily' (still heard in говор, 'local speech, murmur of voices'). Over centuries it replaced older рещи and молвить as the neutral verb 'to speak'.

господи.etymology: Preserved Old Church Slavonic and Old East Slavic vocative singular (господи! 'O Lord!') of господь ('the Lord, master'), from Proto-Slavic *gospodь ('master, lord of the house, host'). Like боже ('O God!') and отче ('O Father!'), господи survives in modern Russian as one of the few fossilized vocative forms, used as an everyday exclamation.

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

гостеприимство.etymology: A compound modelled on Church Slavonic word-building: гость 'guest' + linking vowel -е- + приим- 'receive, welcome' (related to принимать 'to receive') + abstract noun suffix -ство — literally 'guest-receiving'.

гость.etymology: An inherited Slavic word. In Old Russian, гость could mean a guest, a foreigner or a visiting merchant. Vasmer compares German Gast and Latin hostis, whose senses include foreigner and enemy. These related words show how an outsider could be viewed differently in different languages.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: гость

государство.etymology: Inherited from Middle Russian государство ('sovereignty, realm, state', attested from the 15th century), formed with the suffix -ство from государь ('sovereign, lord, monarch'), which contracted in East Slavic from earlier господарь ('lord, master'), derived from господь ('lord, master', Proto-Slavic *gospodь).

готовиться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive verb formed by adding -ся to готовить ('to prepare; to cook'), derived from готовый ('ready', Old East Slavic готовыи, Proto-Slavic *gotovъ).

градус.etymology: Borrowed as a scholarly term from Latin gradus 'step, rung, degree (on a scale or circle)', from gradi 'to step, walk'.
градус.notes: Covers both compass/geometry angles (на девяносто градусов) and temperature (двадцать градусов тепла).

граница.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic граница (attested from 1375), from Proto-Slavic *granica, built on грань 'edge, boundary marker, facet' + -ица.
граница.notes: Idioms: за границу 'abroad (motion)', за границей 'abroad (location)', из-за границы 'from abroad'. Interestingly, German Grenze was borrowed from Slavic *granica.

гриб.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic грибъ, from Proto-Slavic *gribъ ('mushroom, fungus', especially boletus). Vasmer connects *gribъ with the Slavic verb грести / гребу ('to scrape, dig, rake up the earth', Proto-Slavic *grebti), referring to how mushrooms push up through the forest soil and leaf litter (or are dug out of moss).

громко.etymology: Adverb formed from the short neuter of громкий ('loud'), derived from гром ('thunder'), inherited from Old East Slavic громъ and Proto-Slavic *gromъ ('thunder, loud rumbling').

грубо.etymology: Adverb formed from грубый ('coarse, rough, rude'), inherited from Old East Slavic грубыи ('coarse, unrefined, ignorant'), from Proto-Slavic *grǫbъ ('coarse, thick, rough', compare Polish gruby 'thick, fat, coarse' and Lithuanian grumbùs 'rough, uneven, calloused').

грустный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from грусть ('sadness, melancholy'), inherited from Old East Slavic грусть (and Old Church Slavonic гроусть 'grief, sorrow'), from Proto-Slavic *grustь, originally derived from *gruda / *gruzti ('to gnaw, crush, weigh heavily upon the heart', related to грызть 'to gnaw' and Lithuanian graudùs 'heartbreaking, sad, brittle').
грустный.notes: The **т** in the cluster **-стн-** is silent in pronunciation: **[гру́сный]**.

грязный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from грязь ('mud, dirt, mire'), inherited from Old East Slavic грязь, from Proto-Slavic *gręzь ('mud, mire, bog'), derived from the nasal-vowel verb *gręznǫti ('to sink into mud or mire', Russian погрязнуть, cognate with Lithuanian grim̃zti 'to sink into water or mud').

history.meaning: to sink in mire → mud, mire

губернатор.etymology: Borrowed under Peter the Great (early 18th century, when Russia was divided into губернии in 1708) via Polish gubernator from Latin gubernātor ('helmsman, pilot of a ship; ruler, governor'), from gubernāre ('to steer a ship, govern'), itself an ancient borrowing from Greek κυβερνάω (kybernáō, 'to steer').

history.meaning: to steer a ship → helmsman, governor

гусь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гусь, from Proto-Slavic *gǫsь ('goose'), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰh₂éns ('goose'; compare German Gans, English goose, Latin ānser, and Ancient Greek χήν).

дама.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via French dame (and German Dame / Polish dama) from Latin domina ('mistress of a household, lady'), feminine of dominus ('master, lord', from domus 'house'). Denotes both a lady and the queen in playing cards or chess.

дверь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic двьрь (frequently plural двьри for double gates), from Proto-Slavic *dvьrь, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwōr ('door, gate'), cognate with English door, German Tür, Latin foris, and Sanskrit dvār.

дебаты.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via French débats (plural of débat 'discussion, parliamentary debate') or English debates, from Old French debatre ('to fight out, argue, discuss', from de- + batre 'to beat', from Latin battere / battuere).

девочка.etymology: Double diminutive formed from девка ('girl, maid') + suffix -очка, ultimately from дева ('maiden, virgin'), inherited from Old East Slavic дѣва and Proto-Slavic *děva. In modern standard Russian, девочка is the neutral everyday word for a female child ('little girl'), while девка became rustic or pejorative.

дед.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дѣдъ, from Proto-Slavic *dědъ ('grandfather, ancestor, old man'), originating as an expressive reduplicated nursery word (*dē-d-) with close Baltic relatives (Lithuanian dė̃dė 'uncle, old man') and Greek τήθη ('grandmother').

действительно.etymology: Adverb derived from действительный ('real, actual, valid'), formed from действие ('action, effect, reality'), an Old Church Slavonic derivative of дѣяти ('to do, act', from Proto-Slavic *dějati, cognate with English do).

действовать.etymology: Denominative verb formed with the suffix -овать from действие / действо ('action, deed, operation'), borrowed via Old Church Slavonic дѣиство from Proto-Slavic *dějьstvo, built on *dějati ('to do, act', cognate with дело 'deed, business').

деловой.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -овой from дело ('deed, work, business, affair'), inherited from Old East Slavic дѣло, from Proto-Slavic *dělo ('deed, work', built on *děti 'to do, place' with the instrument/result suffix *-lo).

день.etymology: An inherited Slavic word for day, recorded in Old Russian and Old Church Slavonic. Vasmer compares Baltic and other Indo-European relatives. The reduced vowel in the older form helps explain the alternation between день and forms such as дня.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: день

день.notes:
- The vowel is dropped in most forms: день, but дня, дню.
- *День рождения* = birthday; *добрый день* = good afternoon.

деньги.etymology: Plural of historical деньга (attested in 14th-century Old Russian), borrowed from Turkic (compare Tatar täŋkä and Kazakh теңге), originally denoting a stamped silver coin. As small copper деньга coins lost value, the plural деньги became the general word for money.
деньги.notes: Plural-only in modern Russian: **деньги лежат**, genitive **денег**.

дерево.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дерево (with East Slavic pleophony -ере-; compare Old Church Slavonic дрѣво), from Proto-Slavic *dervo, from Proto-Indo-European *dóru / *dréwo- ('tree, oak, wood'), cognate with English tree.

десерт.etymology: Borrowed from French dessert 'sweet course at the end of a meal', from desservir 'to clear the table' (des- 'un-' + servir 'to serve'), since dessert was brought out once the main dishes had been cleared.

дешёвый.etymology: Attested in Old Russian дешевыи from the 15th century. Its deeper origin is uncertain: Vasmer reviews and cautions against several competing proposals, including a derivation from десить ('to find, obtain', Old Church Slavonic десити) or a borrowing from an Eastern trade term.

диван.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French divan and Turkish divan from Persian دیوان (dīvān, 'bundle of written sheets, register, council of state, council chamber lined with cushioned benches along the walls'). From the long cushioned seating in an Ottoman council hall, the word came to mean a 'sofa, couch' across Europe and Russia.

history.meaning: state council hall → cushioned bench along its walls

дисциплина.etymology: Borrowed via Polish dyscyplina and German Disziplin from Latin disciplīna ('instruction, teaching, branch of learning; orderly conduct, military or monastic order'), derived from discipulus ('pupil, learner'), from discere ('to learn').

history.meaning: to learn → pupil → instruction, orderly training

добавить.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix до- ('up to a measure, additionally') and the archaic causative stem бавить ('to cause to be, increase, prolong', preserved in прибавить, убавить, избавить, and разбавить), which goes back to Proto-Slavic *baviti, the old o-grade causative of *byti ('to be', Russian быть).

history.meaning: to be → to cause to be, make more

morphemes.meaning: cause to be / increase (historical causative of быть)

добавлять.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of добавить ('to add, supplement'), formed with the labial epenthetic -л- and imperfective suffix -я- from до- + бавить (historical causative of быть 'to be', Proto-Slavic *baviti 'to cause to be, increase').

доверять.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of доверить ('to entrust, confide, trust'), formed from the prefix до- and верить ('to believe, trust', from вера 'faith, trust', Proto-Slavic *věra).

довольно.etymology: Adverb and predicate formed from довольный ('satisfied, content; sufficient'), derived from Old East Slavic доволъ ('sufficiency, abundance'), built from до ('up to') + воля ('will, wish', Proto-Slavic *voľa), literally 'up to one's wish or heart's content'. Functions as a degree adverb ('quite, rather, fairly'), an exclamation ('enough!'), and a predicate ('pleased').

history.meaning: up to one's wish → sufficiency → sufficient, content

дождь.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dъždžь (Old East Slavic дъжчь; modern spelling дождь follows Church Slavonic tradition). Vasmer favours reconstructing an older Indo-European compound *dus-dyu- ('bad/cloudy sky', built on the sky root *dyew-), though the pre-Slavic etymology retains some debate.

доказать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix до- ('up to the end, thoroughly') and казать ('to show, point out, state', from Proto-Slavic *kazati). Literally, 'to show all the way through, demonstrate conclusively, prove'.

доктор.etymology: Borrowed via Polish doktor or German Doktor from Latin doctor ('teacher, instructor; holder of the highest university degree'), agent noun from docēre ('to teach'). As with English doctor, the academic title of a Doctor of Medicine became the everyday word for a physician.

долг.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дългъ (and Old Church Slavonic длъгъ 'debt, duty'), from Proto-Slavic *dъlgъ ('debt, obligation'). Vasmer compares Gothic dulgs ('debt'), noting an early shared Germanic-Slavic legal/economic term.

дом.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic домъ, from Proto-Slavic *domъ, from Proto-Indo-European *dómh₂os ('house, household'), directly cognate with Latin domus (whence English domestic), Ancient Greek δόμος, and Sanskrit dáma.

домашний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic домашнии ('of the house, domestic'), formed from the archaic adverb дома ('at home') / *domašь (from домъ / дом 'house, home', Proto-Slavic *domъ, PIE *dómh₂os, cognate with Latin domus) + the soft relational adjectival suffix -ний.

допустить.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix до- ('up to') and пустить ('to let go, allow', from Proto-Slavic *pustiti). Literally 'to let someone come up to a place, grant access', whence 'to allow, permit, admit (a possibility), or commit (an error: допустить ошибку)'.

history.meaning: to allow, admit; to suppose (допустим 'let's suppose')

дорого.etymology: Adverb and predicate formed from the neuter short form of дорогой ('dear, precious, expensive'), inherited from Old East Slavic дорогыи (showing East Slavic pleophony -оро-; compare Old Church Slavonic драгъ and Polish drogi), from Proto-Slavic *dorgъ ('dear, precious, high-priced').

дочка.etymology: Affectionate diminutive of дочь ('daughter'), inherited from Old East Slavic дочка (from дъчи, genitive дъчере) with the diminutive suffix -ка.

дочь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дъчи (accusative дъчерь, which reshaped the modern nominative дочь, while the archaic consonant stem -ер- is preserved in the oblique cases дочери, дочерью, дочерей), from Proto-Slavic *dъkti (genitive *dъktere), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰugh₂tḗr ('daughter'; compare Lithuanian duktė̃, Ancient Greek θυγάτηρ, Sanskrit duhitṛ́, German Tochter, and English daughter).

дрова.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дръва ('firewood', plural of дръво 'tree, wood'), from Proto-Slavic *dьrva (nominative plural of *dьrvo / *dervo 'tree, wood', Russian дерево), from Proto-Indo-European *dóru / genitive *dréws ('tree, wood, oak'; cognate with English tree, Welsh derwen 'oak', and Ancient Greek δόρυ 'wood, spear' / δρῦς 'oak'). In Russian, singular дерево means 'living tree / wood as material', while the old zero-grade plural дрова specialized to mean 'split firewood'.

дурак.etymology: Attested in Russian since the 14th–15th centuries (initially often as a protective non-calendar secular name Дурак given to ward off evil spirits, before becoming the common word for 'fool'). Formed with the suffix -ак from the Slavic adjective дурый ('foolish, wild, crazed', compare dialectal дурь 'folly', Ukrainian дурний 'stupid', and Lithuanian padùrmai 'wildly, impetuously').

дурацкий.etymology: Adjective formed from дурак ('fool, idiot') + the adjectival suffix -ский (where к + -ский regularly fuses into -цкий). Literally, 'befitting a fool, foolish, stupid, ridiculous'.

духовка.etymology: Coined in Russian as a compact everyday noun from духовой ('heated by hot enclosed air', in духовая печь 'hot-air baking oven') + -ка, ultimately from дух 'breath, air, heat'.
духовка.notes: In modern Russian kitchens духовка means the enclosed baking oven of a cooker, whereas печь often suggests a traditional masonry stove or bakery oven.

душа.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic душа (and Old Church Slavonic доуша), from Proto-Slavic *duša ('breath, vital spirit, soul'), formed from *duxъ ('breath, spirit, air', Russian дух) with the suffix *-ja (where *xj palatalized to *š). Cognate with Lithuanian daũsos ('air') and Gothic dius ('breathing creature, wild animal', English deer), from PIE *dʰewh₂- ('to breathe, smoke, blow').

дым.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дымъ (and Old Church Slavonic дꙑмъ), from Proto-Slavic *dymъ ('smoke'), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós ('smoke, vapor, breath'; exact cognate with Lithuanian dū́mai, Sanskrit dhūmá-, Latin fūmus, and Ancient Greek θυμός 'breath, spirit').

ерунда.etymology: Emerged in 19th-century Russian seminary, student, and journalistic slang meaning 'nonsense, rubbish, trifle'. Commonly traced by Vasmer and Chernykh to Russian Orthodox seminary jargon adapting Latin gerundium ('the gerund', a grammatical topic notorious among schoolboys for tedious rules), possibly blended with dialectal ерунда / еранда ('watered-down kvass, weak brew, idler').

жадина.etymology: Common-gender colloquial noun formed with the expressive personal suffix -ина from жадный ('greedy, stingy', from Proto-Slavic *žędьnъ).

жадный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жадьныи ('thirsty, craving, eager'), from Proto-Slavic *žędьnъ, derived from the same nasal-vowel root as жажда ('thirst, craving', Old Church Slavonic жѧжда, Proto-Slavic *žędja, cognate with Lithuanian pasigendù 'to miss, long for'). Originally meaning 'thirsty, hungering for' (still its meaning in Polish żądny 'eager for'), in Russian жадный specialized to mean 'greedy, stingy'.

жалко.etymology: Impersonal predicate and adverb formed from the neuter short form of жалкий ('pitiful, pathetic; originally evoking pity or sorrow'), derived from жаль ('pity, grief, sorrow'), inherited from Old East Slavic жаль and Proto-Slavic *žalь ('sharp pain, grief').

history.meaning: it is a pity; (with dative + accusative) to feel sorry for

ждать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жьдати, from Proto-Slavic *žьdati ('to wait, expect'), cognate with Lithuanian geĩsti ('to desire, long for'). The old short yer vowel ь disappeared in weak position, leaving the consonant cluster жд-.

желать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic желати (and Old Church Slavonic желати / желѣти 'to wish, desire, grieve for'), from Proto-Slavic *želati / *želěti ('to long for, desire'), related to жаль ('grief, longing, pity') from a root meaning 'sharp longing or ache'.

желток.etymology: Formed from жёлтый 'yellow' + noun suffix -ок: literally 'the yellow part' of an egg, parallel to белок ('egg white', from белый 'white').
желток.notes: Fleeting о drops in oblique forms: желток -> желтка, желтков.

жестокий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жестокыи (and Old Church Slavonic жесточь / жестокъ), originally meaning physically 'hard, stiff, rigid, unyielding' (a sense still preserved in its paronym жёсткий 'hard, stiff, tough', as in жёсткий матрас or жёсткое мясо). Derived from Proto-Slavic *žestъ / *žestokъ ('hard, stiff'); in standard Russian, жёсткий kept the physical sense 'hard, stiff', while жестокий specialized in the moral sense 'hard-hearted, cruel, fierce, severe'.

жесть.etymology: Borrowed from a Turkic word for sheet metal or brass — compare Tatar җиз and Kazakh жез ('brass, copper alloy') — and adapted in Russian for thin tinned sheet iron.

живо.etymology: Adverb formed from the neuter short form of живой ('alive, lively, brisk'), inherited from Old East Slavic живъ, from Proto-Slavic *živъ ('alive, living'), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós ('alive'; compare Latin vīvus, Lithuanian gývas, Sanskrit jīvá-, and English quick).

жильё.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic жилье, formed with the collective/place suffix -ьё from жилой ('inhabited, residential', historically the past participle жилъ of жить 'to live, dwell', from Proto-Slavic *žiti).

жить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жити (present живу), from Proto-Slavic *žiti, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃w- ('to live'), cognate with Latin vīvō, Ancient Greek βίος, Sanskrit jīvati, and English quick (in its older sense 'living').

журналист.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century from French journaliste ('writer for a periodical or newspaper'), derived from journal ('daily newspaper, diary'), from Old French jornal and Late Latin diurnālis ('daily'), from Latin diēs ('day').

забирать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of забрать ('to take away, pick up, collect'), formed from the prefix за- and -бирать, the iterative stem (with lengthened zero-grade vowel -ир-) of брать ('to take', from Proto-Slavic *bьrati / *birati).

history.meaning: to take away, pick up, collect

заболеть.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the inceptive prefix за- ('beginning of a state') and болеть ('to be ill, hurt'), derived from боль ('pain, illness', from Proto-Slavic *bolь).

history.meaning: to fall ill, get sick; to start hurting

заведение.etymology: Verbal noun formed from завести ('to lead in; to establish, set up, found'), built from за- + вести ('to lead', Proto-Slavic *vesti). In the 18th century, заведение acquired the institutional sense 'something set up or established: an educational institution, public house, restaurant, or establishment' (учебное заведение, питейное заведение).

завидовать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic завидовати ('to envy, begrudge'), derived from зависть / завидѣти ('to look askance at, envy'), formed from the prefix за- and видѣти ('to see, look at', Russian видеть, Proto-Slavic *zaviděti). Exact structural and semantic parallel to Latin invidēre ('to look upon with malice, envy', from in- + vidēre).

history.meaning: to look askance/covetously at → to envy
to envy, be jealous of (+ dat.)

завтрак.etymology: Formed within East Slavic from the prepositional phrase за утро ('for/in the morning') with suffix -ок (compare dialectal заутрок), parallel to завтра ('tomorrow', originally 'into the next morning'). The initial cluster simplified in speech into завтрак.

задавать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of задать ('to set, assign a task; to pose a question'), formed from the prefix за- and давать ('to give', iterative of дать, from Proto-Slavic *davati).

задание.etymology: Verbal noun formed with the suffix -ние from задать ('to assign, set a task', from за- + дать 'to give'). Denotes something assigned to be done: a school assignment, work task, or special mission.

закрытый.etymology: Adjectival passive participle of закрыть ('to close, shut, cover'), formed from the prefix за- and крыть ('to cover, roof', inherited from Old East Slavic крыти, Proto-Slavic *kryti).

заменить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix за- ('in place of') and менить ('to change, exchange'), derived from мена ('exchange, barter', from Proto-Slavic *měna, cognate with Lithuanian mainas 'exchange').

заместитель.etymology: Agent noun formed with the suffix -тель from заместить ('to take the place of, replace, act for'), built on за- ('in place of') + место ('place', Old East Slavic мѣсто, Proto-Slavic *město). Literally, 'one who stands in the place of a superior, a deputy or vice-head'.

history.meaning: to take the place of → substitute, deputy

замолчать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the inceptive prefix за- ('entering a state') and молчать ('to be silent'), inherited from Old East Slavic мълчати (and Old Church Slavonic млъчати), from Proto-Slavic *mьlčati ('to be silent').

history.meaning: to fall silent, stop talking, shut up

замуж.etymology: Univerbated adverbial phrase inherited from Old East Slavic за мужь ('behind/for a husband', accusative of motion after the preposition за), preserving the archaic inanimate-like accusative singular form мужь of муж ('husband', Proto-Slavic *mǫžь). In traditional Slavic patriarchal law and custom, a woman married 'behind a husband' (into his household and protection: выйти замуж 'to get married' and быть замужем 'to be married').

history.meaning: to go in marriage behind/to a husband
in marriage (said of a woman getting married)

замёрзнуть.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix за- and мёрзнуть ('to freeze, feel cold'), inherited from Old East Slavic мьрзнути, from Proto-Slavic *mьrznǫti ('to freeze'), related by ablaut to мороз ('frost', from *morzъ with East Slavic pleophony -оро-).

morphemes.meaning: inchoative verb suffix and infinitive ending

занятый.etymology: Adjectival passive participle of занять ('to occupy, take up, borrow'), formed from the prefix за- and the Proto-Slavic root *jęti ('to take', Old East Slavic яти). In predicate position, the short form занят / занята / заняты ('busy, occupied') is standard.

запретить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic запрѣтити ('to threaten, enjoin sternly, forbid'), formed from за- and прѣтити ('to threaten, restrain, warn', from Proto-Slavic *pertiti). The stem shows the Church Slavonic treatment прѣ- (whereas native East Slavic had перетить 'to obstruct, oppose').

заработать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix за- and работать ('to work', from работа 'work', Proto-Slavic *orbota). Combines two productive meanings of the prefix за-: (1) 'to acquire or earn through working' (заработать деньги) and (2) 'to begin working or functioning' (мотор заработал).

history.meaning: to earn by working; to start working

зарплата.etymology: 20th-century syllabic abbreviation (stump compound) of заработная плата ('earned pay, wages'), compounded from заработный ('earned by work', from заработать 'to earn') + плата ('pay, payment', from платить 'to pay').

заявление.etymology: Verbal noun formed from заявить ('to declare, announce, state officially'), built from the prefix за- and явить ('to show, manifest, make public', from Proto-Slavic *javiti 'to make manifest').

history.meaning: to declare → official statement, written application, police report

здорово.etymology: Formed from the neuter short form of здоровый ('healthy, robust, big, fine'), inherited from Old East Slavic съдоровъ (displaying East Slavic pleophony -оро-), from Proto-Slavic *sъdorvъ ('made of good wood, sound, healthy', from *sъ- 'good' + *dervo 'tree, wood'). With stress on the first syllable (**здо́рово**), it functions as an enthusiastic colloquial evaluation ('great, cool, awesome!'); with stress on the second syllable (**здоро́во**), it is a colloquial greeting ('hi, hello!').

здоровье.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съдоровье (showing East Slavic pleophony -оро-), formed with the abstract neuter suffix -ье (*-ьje) from съдоровъ / здоровый ('healthy, sound'), from Proto-Slavic *sъdorvъ ('of good wood/timber, robust', from *sъ- 'good' + *dervo 'tree, wood').
здоровье.notes: Used in the standard toast **За здоровье!** ('To your health!') and in **На здоровье!** ('You're welcome!', said in reply to thanks for food or hospitality).

здравствуй.etymology: Second-person singular imperative of здравствовать ('to be in good health, thrive'), formed on the Old Church Slavonic stem здрав- (corresponding to native East Slavic здоров- in здоровый), from Proto-Slavic *sъdorvъ ('sound, healthy'). Literally, здравствуй! is a wish meaning 'be healthy!'.

history.meaning: healthy → to be in good health

здравствуй.notes: The first **в** is silent in pronunciation: **[здра́ствуй]**.

здравствуйте.etymology: Grammatically the formal plural imperative of здравствовать ('to thrive, be in good health'), so greeting someone with Здравствуйте! literally wishes 'be healthy!'. The root здрав- is the Church Slavonic counterpart of native East Slavic здоров- (здоровый), from Proto-Slavic *sъdorvъ ('sound, sturdy', literally 'of good wood', built on *sъ- 'good' + *dervo 'tree, timber').

history.meaning: healthy → to be in good health

здравствуйте.notes: Pronounced with a silent first в (sounded like 'zdrastvuyte'). Use singular *Здравствуй* with one close friend or relative.

зеркало.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic зеркало (alongside Church Slavonic зерцало), from Proto-Slavic *zьrkadlo, built from the gaze root *zьrěti ('to look, behold') plus the tool suffix *-dlo (regularly becoming -ло in East Slavic): literally 'a looking-tool'.

злой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic зълъ (long form зълыи), from Proto-Slavic *zъlъ ('bad, evil, angry, crooked'), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰwel- ('to bend, curve, deviate from the right path'; compare Lithuanian Pa-žulnùs 'sloping, crooked', Avestan zūrah- 'deceit, wrong', and Sanskrit hválati 'goes astray').

зря.etymology: Historically the fossilized present active participle (gerund) of the archaic verb зреть ('to look, see', Old East Slavic зьрѣти, Proto-Slavic *zьrěti). In the phrase не зря ('not looking blindly, not without reason'), зря shifted by back-formation or from 'just looking on idly / at random without thinking' to its modern meaning 'in vain, for nothing, pointlessly'.

history.meaning: at random, without thinking → in vain, for nothing

зуб.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic зубъ (and Old Church Slavonic зѫбъ), from Proto-Slavic *zǫbъ ('tooth'), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos ('peg, row of teeth, tooth', from *ǵembʰ- 'to bite, snap'; exact cognate with Ancient Greek γόμφος 'peg, molar', Sanskrit jámbha- 'tooth, tusk', Lithuanian žam̃bas 'sharp edge', and English comb).

игра.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic игра ('game, play, dance, festivity'), from Proto-Slavic *jьgra ('play, game, dance'). Deeper Indo-European etymology is debated (Vasmer discusses proposed connections to Sanskrit éjati 'stirs, moves' and Old Norse eikinn 'wild, lively').

идиот.etymology: Borrowed via French idiot or German Idiot (and Late Latin idiōta 'uneducated person, layman') from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, 'private citizen not holding public office; layman, unskilled person'), derived from ἴδιος (ídios, 'one's own, private').

history.meaning: private → private citizen, layman, ignorant person

идти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ити (present иду), from Proto-Slavic *iti, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁éyti ('to go'; compare Latin īre and Lithuanian eĩti). Its past tense шёл, шла, шли comes from a separate suppletive Slavic stem *šьd- (related to ходить).

известный.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic извѣстьнъ ('known for certain, well-known, reliable'), derived from извѣсть / вѣсть ('news, knowledge, message', Russian весть), from Proto-Slavic *věstь (built on *věděti 'to know', PIE *weyd-).

изменить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic измѣнити (and Old Church Slavonic измѣнити 'to exchange, alter'), formed from из- ('out') + мѣнити ('to change, exchange', from мѣна 'exchange, alternation', Proto-Slavic *měna). With an accusative object (изменить план), it means 'to change, alter'; with a dative object (изменить мужу / родине), it means 'to betray, be unfaithful to, cheat on'.

history.meaning: to change (+ acc.); to betray, cheat on (+ dat.)

измениться.etymology: Perfective reflexive/intransitive verb formed by adding -ся to изменить ('to change, alter'), derived from из- + менить (from Proto-Slavic *měna 'change, exchange').

иметь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic имѣти (and Old Church Slavonic имѣти), from Proto-Slavic *iměti ('to have, hold'), a stative verb built on the same Indo-European root as *jęti ('to take', compare Latin emō 'to take, buy'). Unlike Western European languages, Russian generally expresses everyday possession with у меня есть rather than иметь, reserving иметь for abstract and formal collocations.
иметь.notes: Used chiefly in set phrases such as **иметь право** ('to have the right'), **иметь в виду** ('to mean, have in mind'), and **иметь значение** ('to matter').

иначе.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic инако / иначе ('otherwise, in another way'), comparative/adverbial formation from инъ / иной ('other, another'), from Proto-Slavic *inъ ('one, other', cognate with Latin ūnus and English one).
иначе.notes: Both stress patterns are accepted in standard Russian: **и́наче** and **ина́че** (with **так или ина́че** 'one way or another' always stressed on the middle syllable).

инвалид.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (originally referring to disabled war veterans, on the model of Paris's Hôtel des Invalides) from French invalide ('infirm, disabled soldier'), from Latin invalidus ('weak, infirm, powerless'), formed from in- ('not') + validus ('strong, healthy', from valēre 'to be strong').

history.meaning: disabled veteran → person with a disability

интересовать.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (modeled on French intéresser and German interessieren) from интерес ('interest') + the verbal suffix -овать, ultimately from Latin interesse ('to be between, make a difference, concern, be of importance').

history.meaning: to concern, be of importance → to interest

интернет.etymology: Borrowed in the 1990s from English Internet, shortened from internetwork ('interconnected network of computer networks'), formed from the Latin prefix inter- ('between, among') + English network.

информация.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish informacja or German Information from Latin īnfōrmātiō ('outline, concept, instruction, explanation'), derived from īnfōrmāre ('to shape, fashion, instruct, educate', from in- 'into' + fōrma 'form, shape').

history.meaning: to give form to, instruct → concept, instruction

искренне.etymology: Adverb formed from искренний ('sincere, heartfelt'), which goes back to Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic искрьнии ('near, neighboring, close, intimate'), derived from the archaic adverb/preposition искрь ('near, close by'). The deeper origin of *jьz-krь connects to *krai / *krь ('edge, side', compare край): originally 'standing right beside one, close at hand', whence 'intimate, open-hearted, sincere'.

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

искусство.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic искоусьство ('trial, test, experience, mastery, skill'), formed with the suffix -ство from искоусъ ('trial, test, probation') and искоусити ('to test, try', from Proto-Slavic *jьzkusiti; *kusiti is an early borrowing from Gothic kausjan 'to taste, test, try', cognate with English choose). From 'tested mastery and skill', in the 18th century искусство acquired the aesthetic sense 'fine art' (on the model of German Kunst and French art).

использовать.etymology: Biaspectual verb formed from the prefix из- / ис- ('out') + пользовать ('to benefit, use, treat'), derived from польза ('use, benefit, advantage'), which goes back to Old East Slavic польга / польза ('ease, relief, benefit'), from Proto-Slavic *polьga (built on the root *lьg- 'light, easy', as in лёгкий 'light, easy' and льгота 'privilege, relief').

испортить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix из- / ис- ('out, completely') and портить ('to spoil, ruin, damage'). The base verb портить (attested in Old Russian портити) is derived by Vasmer from портъ ('piece of cut cloth, coarse garment', preserved in портной 'tailor'), originally meaning 'to cut or tear cloth to shreds, mar, ruin'.

history.meaning: cut piece of cloth → to cut up, mar, spoil

исправить.etymology: Borrowed from or modeled on Old Church Slavonic исправити ('to straighten out, set right, correct'), formed from из- / ис- ('out') + правити ('to make straight, direct', from правъ / правый 'straight, right', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

как-то.etymology: Indefinite adverb formed by attaching the indefinite enclitic particle -то (historically the neuter demonstrative pronoun то 'that') to как ('how', from Proto-Slavic *kako).

history.meaning: somehow, sort of; once, one day

какой-нибудь.etymology: Indefinite pronoun formed from какой ('what kind of, which', from Proto-Slavic *kakъ) and the indefinite enclitic particle -нибудь, historically the univerbated phrase ни будь ('be it whatever it may', from ни + будь, the 2nd sg. imperative of быть 'to be').

камера.etymology: Borrowed via German Kamera / Kammer and Polish kamera from Latin camera ('vaulted room, arched chamber'), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, 'anything with an arched cover, vaulted chamber'). In Russian, камера preserves both the older architectural sense ('vaulted cell, prison cell, tire inner tube') and the modern sense ('photographic or video camera', shortened from camera obscura 'dark chamber').

history.meaning: chamber, prison cell; camera (from camera obscura)

кандидат.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Kandidat or Polish kandydat from Latin candidātus ('one clothed in white'), derived from candidus ('shining white'). In ancient Rome, office-seekers wore a bleached white toga (toga candida) in the Forum to symbolize purity and integrity.

history.meaning: gleaming white → office-seeker wearing a white toga

кандидатура.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via German Kandidatur or French candidature, formed with the Medieval Latin office/status suffix -ūra from Latin candidātus ('candidate, office-seeker dressed in a white toga').

капитан.etymology: Borrowed via Polish kapitan from Late Latin capitaneus 'chief, commander', formed on Latin caput 'head'.

капсула.etymology: Borrowed from Latin capsula 'small box or chest', a diminutive of capsa 'box, case for scrolls'. Through French and Italian cousins of capsa, it is a distant doublet of касса and кассета.

капучино.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from Italian cappuccino ('espresso with steamed milk foam'), literally 'Capuchin friar' (from cappuccio 'hood, cowl', because the reddish-brown color of espresso mixed with milk resembled the habit worn by friars of the Capuchin order, and via Viennese Kapuziner coffee).

history.meaning: hood → Capuchin friar → espresso with foamed milk

карандаш.etymology: Borrowed in the sixteenth or seventeenth century from Turkic *qara tas ('black stone, black slate, graphite'), a compound of kara 'black' + tas 'stone', with an intrusive -н- in Russian pronunciation.
карандаш.notes: Writing in pencil takes the instrumental case in Russian: написать карандашом 'to write in pencil'.

картина.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) from Italian cartina ('fine paper, small sheet, print'), a diminutive of carta ('paper, card, chart'), from Latin charta and Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, 'sheet of papyrus'). In Russian, картина expanded from an engraving or print on paper to any painting, picture, or motion picture.

картограф.etymology: An international scholarly compound combining карта 'map, chart' + Greek-derived -граф 'one who writes or draws' (from graphein 'to write, draw').

картография.etymology: Borrowed from French cartographie, a scholarly compound formed from Ancient Greek khartes ('sheet of papyrus, map') + -graphia ('drawing, writing').

картошка.etymology: Colloquial and everyday collective/diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from картофель ('potatoes'), borrowed in the 18th century from German Kartoffel (earlier Tartuffel, altered by dissimilation of t-t > k-t from Italian tartufolo 'little truffle', because potato tubers grow underground like truffles).

кастрюля.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via German Kastrol, a regional variant of Kasserolle, which comes from French casserole 'saucepan' (a diminutive of casse 'pan').

качество.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic качьство ('quality, nature, sort'), formed as a calque of Ancient Greek ποιότης (poiótēs, coined by Plato from ποῖος 'of what kind?', just as Cicero coined Latin quālitās from quālis 'of what kind?'), built from the Slavic interrogative pronoun какъ ('of what kind, how', Russian какой) + the abstract suffix -ьство (-ство), with palatalization of к > ч.

каша.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic каша ('porridge, cooked grain'), from Proto-Slavic *kaša ('porridge, gruel'), cognate with Lithuanian košė ('porridge, mash', from kirti / košti 'to strain, filter').

квота.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th or early 20th century via German Quote or English quota from Medieval Latin quota (short for quota pars 'how great a part, proportional share'), from Latin quot ('how many').

кино.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century from German Kino, a clipping of Kinematograph (compare French cinématographe, coined by the Lumière brothers in the 1890s), from Ancient Greek κίνημα (kínēma, 'movement', from κινέω 'to move') + γράφω (gráphō, 'to write, record').
кино.notes: Indeclinable neuter noun in Russian: **пойти в кино**, **смотреть старое кино**.

кирпич.etymology: Borrowed from Turkic — compare Turkish kerpic, Tatar кирпеч, and Kazakh кірпіш ('sun-dried or fired clay brick') — attested in East Slavic since late medieval building accounts.
кирпич.notes: Stress stays on the ending throughout its declension: кирпич, кирпича, кирпичи, кирпичей.

клад.etymology: Native East Slavic noun built on the root of класть ('to lay, put, stow away'): literally something laid away in a secret spot for safekeeping, hence 'buried treasure, hoard'.

класс.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Klasse and French classe from Latin classis ('one of the six property divisions of Roman citizens; fleet, army; school class, rank, category'). In colloquial modern Russian, класс! is also used as an exclamation meaning 'top-class, cool, awesome!'.

кластер.etymology: Borrowed in the second half of the 20th century (first in astronomy, physics, and computing, later in economics and regional policy) from English cluster ('bunch, group of similar things growing or held together'), from Old English clyster ('bunch, cluster').

клиент.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century via German Klient or French client from Latin cliēns (genitive clientis, 'dependent, follower under the protection of a Roman patrician patron', later 'legal client, customer'), related to clināre ('to lean on') or cluēre ('to hear, obey').

history.meaning: plebeian under a patron's protection; legal client

клоун.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from English clown ('comic stage rustic, jester, circus clown'), which entered 16th-century English (originally meaning 'clod, boor, country bumpkin') from Low German or Scandinavian (compare Icelandic klunni 'clumsy, boorish fellow' and Low German Klönne).

ключ.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ключь, from Proto-Slavic *kľučь ('hook, wooden bolt, key'), belonging to an Indo-European family for curved bolts and locks (compare Latin clāvis 'key' and claudō 'to close'). In Russian the same word denotes a door key, a musical clef, and a mechanic's wrench.

клякса.etymology: Borrowed from German Klecks 'blot, splatter of ink', from klecksen 'to blot, splash', adapted into Russian as a feminine -а noun.
клякса.notes: Поставить кляксу means 'to make an ink blot' when writing with a dip nib or fountain pen.

клясться.etymology: Reflexive form of клясть ('to curse, execrate'), inherited from Old East Slavic кляти / клятися (1st sg. кльнуся), from Proto-Slavic *klęti sę ('to swear an oath', literally 'to call down a curse upon oneself if one's word is false').

history.meaning: to bind oneself by a curse → to swear an oath

книга.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кънига (often plural кънигы 'letters, scroll, book'), from Proto-Slavic *kъniga. Its ultimate pre-Slavic origin is uncertain: Vasmer discusses proposed wanderword routes through Turkic from East Asian or Near Eastern terms for scrolls without a single proven path.

когда-нибудь.etymology: Indefinite temporal adverb formed from когда ('when', from Old East Slavic къгда, Proto-Slavic *kъgda) + the indefinite enclitic particle -нибудь (from ни будь 'be it whenever it may', 2nd sg. imperative of быть 'to be').

history.meaning: whenever it may be → someday, one day, ever

кое-что.etymology: Indefinite pronoun formed from the prefix кое- (historically the neuter singular кое of the archaic interrogative/relative pronoun коий 'which', Proto-Slavic *kъjь) + что ('what', Proto-Slavic *čьto). Typically implies something specific that the speaker knows about but chooses not to name yet ('something, a thing or two').

колпак.etymology: Attested in Old Russian from the 15th century for a tall pointed felt cap or crown; borrowed from Turkic qalpaq ('tall felt or fur cap'; compare Turkish kalpak, Kazakh қалпақ, and Tatar калпак). In modern Russian, колпак denotes a tall chef's toque (поварской колпак), a nightcap, a fool's cap, or a protective glass/lamp dome.

комната.etymology: Borrowed via Polish and Czech komnata from Old High German kemināta, ultimately from Medieval Latin camīnāta ('a room heated by a fireplace', from Latin camīnus 'hearth, stove'). In older Russian architecture it originally meant a warm, heated chamber, before broadening to any indoor room.

history.meaning: room with a hearth or stove

комната.notes: In hotels, an individual guest room is usually called **номер**, while **комната** names a room in a house or flat.

компас.etymology: Borrowed via German Kompass (and Dutch kompas) from Italian compasso 'divider, mariner's compass', derived from Late Latin compassare 'to pace out, measure around' (com- + passus 'step, pace').
компас.notes: Standard everyday Russian stresses the first syllable ком- in компас.

комплимент.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via German Kompliment and French compliment from Italian complimento ('act of courtesy, polite expression of praise'), from Spanish cumplimiento ('fulfillment of courtesy'), derived from Latin complēre ('to fill up, complete, fulfill one's polite duty'). In restaurant usage, комплимент от шефа (blended with French/English complimentary) also denotes a free appetizer from the chef.

history.meaning: compliment; complimentary dish from the chef

конверт.etymology: Borrowed from French couvert 'envelope, cover; place setting', originally the past participle of couvrir 'to cover' (from Latin cooperire), with an intrusive н added in Russian pronunciation.

кондитер.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (earlier кандитор) from German Konditor ('pastry chef, confectioner'), which was adapted in Renaissance German from Latin condītor ('one who seasons, preserves, or pickles food and fruit'), from condīre ('to season, spice, preserve in sugar').

history.meaning: to season, preserve → maker of preserves and sweets

конкурент.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from German Konkurrent ('competitor, rival'), from Latin concurrēns (genitive concurrentis), present participle of concurrere ('to run together, clash, compete', from com- 'together' + currere 'to run').
