контролировать.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from German kontrollieren (or formed in Russian with -ировать from контроль), from French contrôler ('to verify against a duplicate register, supervise'), from Old French contrerolle ('counter-roll, duplicate ledger used to verify accounts', from contre- + rolle 'scroll, roll').

контроль.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century via French contrôle (or German Kontrolle) from Old French contrerolle ('duplicate register or roll kept to verify the first'), from Medieval Latin contrārotulus (contrā- 'against' + rotulus 'little wheel, scroll, roll').

history.meaning: duplicate scroll used to audit accounts

конфета.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (earlier конфекты) via German Konfekt and Polish konfekty from Italian confetto ('candied fruit, sweetmeat, sugar plum'), from Medieval Latin confectum ('something prepared, medicinal preserve or sweetmeat compounded by an apothecary'), neuter past participle of Latin conficere ('to put together, prepare').

концерт.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Konzert and French concert from Italian concerto ('musical performance, harmony, agreement'), derived from concertāre ('to bring into agreement, harmonize; in Latin, to contend, strive together').

коньяк.etymology: Borrowed from French cognac, named after the town of Cognac in southwestern France (Charente department), where the double-distilled wine brandy has been produced since the 17th century.

history.meaning: town in Charente → brandy from Cognac

копейка.etymology: Shortened from копейная деньга ('lance coin'), introduced during the monetary reform of Elena Glinskaya (mother of Ivan the Terrible) in 1534–1535. The new silver wire coins minted in Moscow depicted the Grand Prince on horseback holding a lance (**копьё**, from Old East Slavic копие, Proto-Slavic *kopьje 'spear, lance'), distinguishing them from older coins showing a saber.

history.meaning: silver coin stamped with a rider holding a lance (копьё)

корж.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from Ukrainian корж 'flat dry cake, baked disc of dough', used in Russian baking for each baked pastry layer of a layered cake or tart base.

корица.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic корица (Proto-Slavic *korica), a diminutive of кора 'tree bark' — literally 'little bark', because cinnamon sticks are dried rolls of inner bark.
корица.notes: The Russian adjective коричневый 'brown' comes directly from корица ('cinnamon-coloured')!

короче.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic короче, the comparative degree of короткий ('short', Old East Slavic коротъкыи, from Proto-Slavic *kortъkъ, comparative *kortje, with East Slavic ч from *tj). In colloquial Russian, короче (short for короче говоря 'speaking more briefly') is ubiquitous as the discourse filler 'in short, anyway, long story short'.

rootFamily.gloss: to stop (Church Slavonic root variant крат-)

костюм.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century from French costume ('customary dress, attire, suit'), which was borrowed from Italian costume ('custom, habit, style of dress'), from Vulgar Latin *cōnsuētūmen (from Classical Latin cōnsuētūdō 'custom, habit').

кофе.etymology: Vasmer traces кофе to English coffee or Dutch koffie, and the wider European word family ultimately to Arabic qahwa. He records the older Russian variants кофей and кофий. The immediate borrowing route is therefore presented as an alternative, not a settled single path.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: кофе

кофе.notes: In formal Russian, кофе is masculine and indeclinable: чёрный кофе, крепкий кофе. The stress stays on the first syllable.

кошмар.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French cauchemar ('nightmare, oppressive dream'), a compound of Old French caucher ('to trample, press down upon', from Latin calcāre 'to tread with the heel') and mare ('night-goblin, incubus', from Germanic/Dutch mare, cognate with the second element of English nightmare).

краситель.etymology: Formed in Russian with the agent/instrument suffix -тель from красить ('to paint, dye, color'), derived from краса ('beauty, bright color', in Old East Slavic especially 'red or bright color', from Proto-Slavic *krasa).

history.meaning: to dye, color → dye, coloring agent

кредит.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Kredit and French crédit from Italian credito ('trust, commercial credit, loan'), from Latin crēditum ('something entrusted, a loan'), neuter past participle of crēdere ('to believe, trust, entrust').

критик.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Kritiker or French critique from Latin criticus, itself from Ancient Greek κριτικός (kritikós, 'able to discern or judge'), derived from κρίνω (krínō, 'to separate, decide, judge').

history.meaning: judge of literature or art, critic

кровь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кры (accusative кръвь, which replaced the old nominative, just as in любовь and церковь), from Proto-Slavic *kry (genitive *krъve, 'blood'), from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂- ('raw flesh, clotted blood, gore'; compare Lithuanian kraũjas 'blood', Sanskrit kravíṣ- 'raw flesh', Latin cruor 'blood from a wound' / crūdus 'raw', and English raw).

круассан.etymology: Borrowed from French croissant ('crescent; crescent-shaped flaky pastry'), originally the present participle of croître ('to grow, wax, as the waxing crescent moon'), from Latin crēscere ('to grow'). The Viennese crescent roll (Kipferl) was popularized in Paris in the 19th century as the croissant.

кружиться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive form of кружить ('to circle, whirl, spin'), a denominative verb formed from круг ('circle, wheel, disk', with г > ж before -и-), inherited from Old East Slavic кругъ and Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ ('circle, ring', cognate with Old Norse hringr and English ring).

history.meaning: circle → to move in a circle
to spin, whirl; (голова кружится) to feel dizzy

крыса.etymology: Attested in Russian from the 16th–17th centuries (earlier крыса / криса; compare dialectal кртыса and Lithuanian kirstùkas 'shrew'). Vasmer connects it with the Proto-Slavic root *krt- / *krys- ('to gnaw, cut, burrow', related to крот 'mole' and Lithuanian kir̃sti 'to cut, bite'). In Russian criminal and prison slang, крыса also means a 'mole, traitor who steals from or informs on his own group'.

крючок.etymology: Diminutive of крюк 'hook' with suffix -ок. Old East Slavic крюкъ was borrowed from Old Norse krokr 'hook, bend' (the same Scandinavian source that gave English crook).

кстати.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase к стати ('to the proper fit, proportion, or occasion'), from the preposition к ('to') and the dative singular of стать ('form, build, stature, fitting moment', derived from стать 'to stand, become', Proto-Slavic *statь). From meaning 'fittingly, at an opportune moment' (это очень кстати), it also grammaticalized into the discourse marker 'by the way, speaking of which'.

history.meaning: to the proper fit or occasion, opportunely

кулинарный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from кулинар / кулинария ('culinary art, cookery'), borrowed in the 19th century via German kulinarisch / French culinaire from Latin culīnārius ('pertaining to the kitchen'), from culīna ('kitchen').

курица.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic курица ('hen, chicken'), formed with the feminine suffix -ица from куръ ('rooster, cock', preserved in курятник 'henhouse' and the proverb попасть как кур во щи), from Proto-Slavic *kurъ ('rooster'), an onomatopoeic formation imitating the bird's crowing.

кухня.etymology: Vasmer records кухня from 1717, with поварня used earlier. He traces the borrowing through Polish and Czech to an Old High German word for kitchen, ultimately from Latin coquina. The Russian word belongs to a much-travelled European kitchen-word family.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: кухня

кушать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кушати / покушати ('to taste, try, test, experience'), from Proto-Slavic *kušati (iterative of *kusiti 'to taste, try', an early borrowing from Gothic kausjan 'to taste, test', from the same root as вкус 'taste' and искусство). From 'tasting or sampling food and drink', кушать became a polite or deferential verb for 'to eat' (traditionally used when inviting guests to eat — Кушайте, пожалуйста! — or when speaking to children).

history.meaning: to eat (polite invitation or with children)

кушать.notes: In careful standard Russian, adults usually say **я ем** (from **есть**) about themselves rather than *я кушаю*, reserving **кушать** for polite invitations (**Кушать подано!**, **Кушайте!**) and children.

лаборатория.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin laboratorium 'workshop, place of scientific work', built on Latin laborare 'to work, take pains' from labor 'toil, effort'.

лезть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣзти (present лѣзу), from Proto-Slavic *lězti ('to climb, crawl, creep'), cognate with Latvian lēzēt ('to slide, creep') and Old Prussian līse ('crawls'). In colloquial Russian, лезть also means 'to barge in, meddle, stick one's nose into' (не лезь не в своё дело).

history.meaning: to climb, reach into; to intrude, meddle

лейтенант.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th–18th century via German Leutnant from French lieutenant ('deputy, officer acting in place of a superior'), a compound of lieu ('place', from Latin locus) + tenant ('holding', present participle of tenir 'to hold', from Latin tenēre), literally 'place-holder'.

лестница.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣствица / лѣстница, from Proto-Slavic *lěstvica, built on the verb лезть (*lězti, 'to climb'). Literally 'something for climbing'; the middle т is silent in modern pronunciation ('lesnitsa').

лечить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣчити ('to heal, cure, treat'), from Proto-Slavic *lěčiti, a denominative verb from *lěkъ ('medicine, remedy, healing charm'; preserved in лекарство 'medicine', Polish lek 'medicine', and Czech lék). Most etymologists (including Vasmer) trace *lěkъ to an early borrowing from Gothic lēkeis ('physician, healer'; compare Old English lǣċe 'physician', archaic English leech). In modern Russian slang, лечить кого-то also means 'to lecture, feed tall tales, try to talk someone into something'.

history.meaning: to treat medically; (slang) to lecture, spin a yarn

личный.etymology: Derived from лицо ('face; person, individual', Old East Slavic лице, Proto-Slavic *lice) with palatalization of ц > ч before the adjectival suffix -ный. As лицо developed the legal and grammatical sense 'person, individual' (influenced by Old Church Slavonic translating Greek πρόσωπον), личный came to mean 'personal, private, individual'.

ложь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лъжь ('lie, falsehood'), from Proto-Slavic *lъžь, a feminine i-stem noun derived from the root of лгать ('to lie', Old East Slavic лъгати, Proto-Slavic *lъgati), from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ- ('to tell a lie'; exact cognate with German Lüge and English lie).

любовница.etymology: Feminine counterpart of любовник ('lover'), formed with the feminine agent suffix -ница from любовный ('amorous, of love'), derived from любовь ('love', Old East Slavic любы / любовь, Proto-Slavic *ľuby).

любовь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic любы (accusative любовь, which replaced the old nominative, just as in кровь and морковь), from Proto-Slavic *ľuby (genitive *ľubъve, 'love, affection'), from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ- ('to care, desire, love'; cognate with English love, German Liebe, and Sanskrit lúbhyati 'desires').
любовь.notes: When used as a common noun ('love'), the vowel **о** is fleeting in oblique cases (**любви́**, **любо́вью**); in the female given name **Любо́вь**, the **о** is retained throughout (**у Любо́ви**).

майор.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century via German Major (and Polish major) from Spanish mayor / French major, shortened from sergeant-major, ultimately from Latin maior ('greater, senior', comparative of magnus 'great').

мало.etymology: Adverb and quantifier formed from the neuter short form of малый ('small, little'), inherited from Old East Slavic мало / малъ, from Proto-Slavic *malъ ('small, little'). Vasmer compares Gothic smals ('small'), Ancient Greek μῆλον ('small cattle, sheep'), and Latin malus.

малыш.etymology: Formed in Russian with the expressive noun suffix -ыш from малый ('small, little'), inherited from Old East Slavic малъ and Proto-Slavic *malъ ('small').

марка.etymology: Borrowed via German Marke 'mark, token, stamp' from French marque, of Germanic origin (akin to mark 'sign, boundary'). Used in Russian both for a postage stamp (почтовая марка) and for a brand or make.

маршрут.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from German Marschroute ('line of march, planned itinerary'), a compound of Marsch ('march') + Route ('road, route'), both originally from French.
маршрут.notes: Everyday Russian uses маршрут for bus and tram lines as well as walking or travel itineraries.

масло.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic масло ('butter, oil'), from Proto-Slavic *maslo (< *maz-slo), built from мазать ('to spread, smear, anoint') plus suffix *-slo: literally 'something spread on bread'.

матч.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th century from English match ('sports contest, game between two matched sides'), from Middle English macche ('equal, opponent, counterpart, contest'), from Old English ġemæcca ('mate, companion, equal').

мать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мати (accusative матерь, which gave the modern nominative мать, while the ancient consonant stem -ер- is preserved in all oblique cases: матери, матерью, матерей), from Proto-Slavic *mati (genitive *matere), from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr ('mother'; compare Sanskrit mātṛ́, Ancient Greek μήτηρ, Latin māter, Lithuanian mótė, German Mutter, and English mother).

машинка.etymology: Diminutive of машина ('machine, engine; car'), formed with the suffix -ка. Base noun машина was borrowed in the Petrine era via German Maschine / French machine from Latin māchina ('device, engine, contrivance'), from Doric Greek μαχανά (mākhaná, Attic μηχανή mēkhanḗ). While машина in everyday Russian came to mean a full-sized 'car, automobile', the diminutive машинка denotes either a 'toy car' or a small household/office appliance (стиральная машинка 'washing machine', пишущая машинка 'typewriter', машинка для стрижки 'hair clippers').

медаль.etymology: Borrowed via French medaille from Italian medaglia 'coin, medallion', going back to Late Latin medalia 'small coin worth half a denarius' (related to Latin medius 'middle, half').

мечеть.etymology: Attested in Old Russian chronicles and travel accounts from the 14th–15th centuries (as мечеть / мизгить), borrowed via Volga Bulgar or Kipchak Turkic mäčät / mäčit from Arabic مَسْجِد (masjid, 'mosque', literally 'place of prostration in prayer', from sajada 'to bow down, prostrate oneself'; the same Arabic word gave Spanish mezquita and English mosque).

миллион.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via French million or German Million from Italian milione (attested in the 13th–14th centuries, famously in Marco Polo's Il Milione), an augmentative of mille ('thousand', from Latin mīlle), literally 'a great thousand' (1,000 × 1,000).

миндаль.etymology: Entered Russian via Old Church Slavonic мигдалъ and Polish migdal from Latin amygdalus and Ancient Greek amygdale 'almond', with the consonant cluster reshaping smoothly to миндаль in East Slavic.

cognates.meaning: almond (via Old French almande from the same Latin word)

миндаль.notes: Used as a collective masculine singular noun in culinary Russian: жареный миндаль 'roasted almonds'.

молодец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic молодьць ('young man, brave warrior, gallant youth'), formed from молодъ / молодой ('young', displaying East Slavic pleophony -оло- from Proto-Slavic *moldъ) + the masculine noun suffix -ец. In folk poetry, добрый молодец meant a 'strapping, valiant youth', which generalized into an exclamation of praise ('well done! good job!').

молоко.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic молоко (showing East Slavic pleophony -оло-; compare Old Church Slavonic млѣко and Polish mleko), from Proto-Slavic *melko. Vasmer compares Proto-Germanic *meluk- (English milk, German Milch), noting that scholars debate whether Slavic borrowed the word early from Germanic or shared an older western Indo-European root.

момент.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via German Moment or French moment from Latin mōmentum ('movement, impulse, brief particle of time', contracted from *movimentum), derived from movēre ('to move').

монастырь.etymology: Borrowed in the Old East Slavic period (attested from the 11th century as манастырь / монастырь) from Byzantine Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion, 'hermitage, monastery'), from μοναστήρ / μοναχός (monakhós, 'monk, solitary'), derived from μόνος (mónos, 'alone, solitary').

монета.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish moneta from Latin moneta 'mint; coined money', named after the temple of Juno Moneta on the Capitoline Hill in Rome, beside which silver coins were struck.

history.meaning: epithet of Juno; the Roman mint; coin

cognates.meaning: place where coins are struck (early Germanic loan from Latin moneta)

мост.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мостъ ('bridge; timber-paved street'), from Proto-Slavic *mostъ. Vasmer connects it most plausibly with метать ('to throw, lay across': logs laid across water or mud), an older sense still visible in мостовая ('cobblestone or paved roadway').

муж.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мужь (and Old Church Slavonic мѫжь 'man, husband'), from Proto-Slavic *mǫžь ('man, male, husband'), from Proto-Indo-European *mon-gʷ-yo- / *man-u- ('man'; compare Sanskrit mányate / mánu-, German Mann, and English man).

мужик.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мужикъ (attested from the 13th–14th centuries), formed with the diminutive/expressive suffix -ик from мужь / муж ('man, husband', Proto-Slavic *mǫžь). Historically denoting a commoner or peasant man as opposed to a nobleman, in modern colloquial Russian мужик means 'guy, bloke' or 'a tough, real man'.

мучить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мучити ('to torment, torture'), a denominative verb from мука ('torment, torture, agony'; note stress **му́ка**, distinct from **мука́** 'flour', though both share the same root!), from Proto-Slavic *mǫka ('torment; flour', originally 'crushing, kneading, pressing', from PIE *menk- 'to knead, crush', cognate with Lithuanian mìnkyti 'to knead dough').

мы.etymology: An inherited Slavic first-person plural pronoun, recorded in Old Church Slavonic as мы. Vasmer compares Baltic relatives, including Lithuanian mes. He discusses possible reshaping of the pronoun by analogy with other grammatical forms; that detail is a proposed historical explanation rather than a simple borrowing story.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: мы

мясной.etymology: Relational adjective inherited from Old East Slavic мясьныи, formed with the suffix -ной from мясо ('meat, flesh'), from Proto-Slavic *męso (cognate with Lithuanian mėsà, Sanskrit māṃsá-, and Gothic mimz).

мясо.etymology: An inherited Slavic word for meat or flesh. Vasmer records it across the Slavic languages and compares Baltic and Indo-Iranian relatives. It belongs to an older inherited word family rather than being a recent Russian borrowing.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: мясо

мясо.notes:
- Common collocations: *жареное мясо* (fried meat), *куриное мясо* (chicken meat).
- Genitive plural *мяс* is rare; the word is mostly used in the singular.

мята.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *męta, an early borrowing from Latin menta 'mint' (with nasal *ę regularly yielding Russian я), which comes from Ancient Greek minthe.

cognates.meaning: aromatic herb (early borrowing from Latin menta)

мята.notes: Comparing Polish mięta (preserving the nasal vowel) with Russian мята nicely illustrates the regular Slavic sound law *ę -> я.

навести.etymology: Perfective verb inherited from Old East Slavic навести (1st sg. наведу), formed from the prefix на- ('onto, upon') and вести ('to lead, conduct', from Proto-Slavic *vesti). Used both literally ('to direct, aim, lead onto; to build a bridge across') and in common idioms such as навести порядок ('to put in order, tidy up') and навести справки ('to make inquiries').

history.meaning: to direct, aim; to establish (навести порядок)

наглый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic наглыи ('sudden, headlong, impetuous'), from Proto-Slavic *naglъ ('sudden, abrupt, rash', compare Polish nagły 'sudden, abrupt, urgent' and Czech náhlý 'sudden'). In Russian, the meaning shifted from acting with 'headlong abruptness' (preserved in нагрянуть) to acting with 'brazen, shameless impudence'.

надеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic надѣти, from Proto-Slavic *naděti ('to put on, place upon'), formed from the prefix *na- ('on, onto') and *děti ('to put, place', Russian деть, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- 'to put, do').
надеть.notes: Standard Russian distinguishes **надеть** ('to put an item of clothing on oneself': *надеть пальто, надеть очки*) from **одеть** ('to dress a person': *одеть ребёнка*).

надоесть.etymology: Formed from the prefix над- / надо- ('over, upon, to excess') and есть ('to eat', Old East Slavic ѣсти, Proto-Slavic *ěsti, from PIE *h₁ed-). Literally 'to eat away at someone, gnaw at someone to excess', whence 'to bore to death, make someone sick and tired of something' (мне это надоело).

history.meaning: to gnaw at, eat away at
to bore, get on someone's nerves, make sick and tired of (+ dat.)

назвать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic назьвати ('to call by name, summon'), formed from the prefix на- and звать ('to call', Old East Slavic зъвати, Proto-Slavic *zъvati, cognate with Sanskrit hváyati 'calls, invokes').

назначить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix на- and значить ('to mark, signify, mean'), derived from знак ('sign, mark', from Proto-Slavic *znakъ, built on *znati 'to know'). Literally, 'to put a mark on, designate for a role or time', whence 'to appoint (to a post), set (a date/meeting), or prescribe (treatment)'.

history.meaning: to appoint, designate, set (a time), prescribe

называться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive/passive verb formed from называть ('to call, name', imperfective of назвать, with lengthened root vowel -ы- from Proto-Slavic *nazyvati, built on *zъvati 'to call'). Means 'to be called, have the name/title of'.

rootFamily.gloss: name, title (of an object, book, restaurant)

найтись.etymology: Perfective reflexive/passive form of найти ('to find', literally 'to come upon by walking', from на- 'onto, upon' + йти / идти 'to go', Old East Slavic наити, Proto-Slavic *najьti). With -сь, найтись means 'to be found, turn up' (and figuratively 'to find the right words, not be at a loss').

rootFamily.gloss: to be located; to be found (impf.)

наказать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic наказати ('to instruct, admonish, teach a lesson'), formed from the prefix на- and казати ('to show, point out, speak', Proto-Slavic *kazati). Up to the 18th century, наказать meant 'to instruct, give orders' (preserved in наказ 'mandate, instruction to a deputy'); from 'teaching someone a stern lesson', it shifted in modern Russian to 'to punish'.

напиток.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic напитокъ, formed with the noun suffix -ок from напить / напиться ('to drink one's fill', passive participle напитый), built from the prefix на- and пить ('to drink', Proto-Slavic *piti).

например.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase на пример ('for an example, after the model of'), formed from the preposition на ('for, onto') + пример ('example, model'), which is derived from примерить ('to try on, measure against', from при- + мерить 'to measure', built on мера 'measure', Proto-Slavic *měra).

напугать.etymology: Perfective counterpart of пугать ('to scare, frighten'), formed with the prefix на- and the expressive East Slavic verb пугать (compare dialectal пуга 'whip; owl' and Ukrainian пугач 'eagle owl', from an onomatopoeic cry *pug- used to startle birds or animals).

нарезать.etymology: Formed from the cumulative prefix на- ('in a quantity, into pieces') and резать ('to cut, slice'), inherited from Old East Slavic рѣзати and Proto-Slavic *rězati ('to cut, carve', cognate with Lithuanian rė́žti 'to cut, incise'). Note that stress distinguishes aspect: perfective **наре́зать** ('to slice up') vs. imperfective **нареза́ть**.

народ.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic народъ ('people, multitude, lineage'), from Proto-Slavic *narodъ, a deverbal noun formed from *naroditi ('to give birth to in numbers, beget, produce'), from *na- + *roditi ('to give birth', Russian родить). Literally, 'that which has been born or grown up together, a generation or people'.

народный.etymology: Relational adjective inherited from Old East Slavic народьныи, formed from народ ('people, nation', from Proto-Slavic *narodъ) + the adjectival suffix -ный.

нарушение.etymology: Verbal noun formed from нарушить ('to break, violate, disturb'), built from на- + рушить ('to break down, tear down, shatter', from Proto-Slavic *rušiti). Just as English speaks of 'breaking' a law or rule, Russian uses нарушить / нарушение for the 'breach or violation' of a rule, law, or order.

history.meaning: to break (a rule/peace) → violation, breach, infringement

настроение.etymology: Verbal noun from настроить ('to tune a musical instrument; to attune, put in a frame of mind'), built from на- + строить ('to arrange, order, build', from Proto-Slavic *strojiti). Just as German Stimmung ('mood') comes from stimmen ('to tune an instrument'), Russian настроение shifted from 'the tuning of strings' to a person's emotional 'mood, frame of mind'.

history.meaning: tuning of a musical instrument → emotional attunement, mood

наступить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic наступити ('to step upon, advance; to come upon'), formed from the prefix на- ('on, onto') and ступить ('to step, tread', from Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti). Has two primary uses in modern Russian: physical ('to step on something', наступить на ногу) and temporal ('to come, set in, arrive', of seasons, times of day, or events: наступила зима).

history.meaning: to step on; to set in
to step on (+ на); to come, arrive (of time/events)

натворить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the cumulative prefix на- ('in a quantity') and творить ('to create, make, do'), inherited from Old East Slavic творити and Proto-Slavic *tvoriti ('to form, shape, make', related to тварь 'creature'). In modern colloquial Russian, натворить specialized in a negative or ironic sense: 'to do something bad, cause a mess or trouble' (Что ты натворил? 'What have you done?!').

history.meaning: to do/make (especially mischief, trouble, or a mess)

научить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic научити, formed from the perfective prefix на- and учить ('to teach', from Proto-Slavic *učiti, causative of the PIE root *h₁ewk- 'to become accustomed, learn').

history.meaning: to teach (someone: acc. + чему: dat. or infinitive)

научиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed by adding -ся ('oneself') to научить ('to teach'), from Old East Slavic научити, built from на- + учить ('to teach', Proto-Slavic *učiti, causative of the PIE root *h₁ewk- 'to become accustomed'). Literally, 'to teach oneself, acquire a skill'.

начальник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic начальникъ (and Old Church Slavonic начѧльникъ 'founder, leader, chief'), formed from начало ('beginning, command, authority', from начать 'to begin', Proto-Slavic *načęti) + the agent suffix -ник.

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

начаться.etymology: Perfective intransitive/reflexive verb formed by adding -ся to начать ('to begin, start'), inherited from Old East Slavic начати, from Proto-Slavic *načęti ('to begin', from *na- + *čęti, related to конец 'end').

не.etymology: The negative particle не is inherited from older Slavic, rather than being a recent borrowing. Vasmer compares negative forms across the Indo-European languages, including Latin ne- and Baltic ne. The Russian particle also appears in word formation, but a prefixed word may develop a meaning of its own.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: не

невозможно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate formed from невозможный ('impossible'), built with the negative prefix не- on возможный ('possible'), which derives from Old Church Slavonic възмощи / возмочь ('to be able, have the power to', from въз- + мощи / мочь 'to be able, can', Proto-Slavic *moťi).

невыезд.etymology: Formed with the negative prefix не- ('non-') from выезд ('departure, exit by vehicle, trip out'), a deverbal noun from выехать ('to drive out, depart', from вы- + ехать 'to go by vehicle', Proto-Slavic *ěxati). Used almost exclusively in the legal formula **подписка о невыезде** ('signed undertaking not to leave town pending trial or investigation').

незнакомец.etymology: Built transparently from не- 'un-, not' + знакомец 'acquaintance' (from знакомый 'familiar, known' + person suffix -ец, ultimately from знать 'to know').

немедленно.etymology: Adverb formed from the adjective немедленный ('immediate, unhesitating'), built with the negative prefix не- on медленный ('slow'), historically a participle related to медлить ('to delay, tarry', from Proto-Slavic *mьdьlъ 'slow, sluggish').

немецкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нѣмьчьскыи ('foreign, Western European, German'), formed from нѣмьць / немец ('German; in medieval Rus', any foreigner speaking an unintelligible Western tongue'), derived with the suffix *-ьcь from нѣмъ / немой ('mute, dumb, unable to speak intelligibly', Proto-Slavic *němъ). Early Slavs contrasted themselves — словене, 'people of the intelligible word (слово)' — with their western neighbors, *němьci ('those who cannot speak [our language]').

history.meaning: mute → speaker of an unintelligible tongue, Germanic neighbor

ненавидеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ненавидѣти (and Old Church Slavonic ненавидѣти 'to hate'), from Proto-Slavic *nenaviděti, formed with the negative prefix *ne- on *naviděti ('to look gladly upon, favor'), itself from *na- ('upon') + *viděti ('to see, look at', Russian видеть). Literally, 'not to bear looking at someone' (compare Latin invidia 'envy', from in- + vidēre).

history.meaning: to be unable to look upon → to hate

неправда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic неправьда ('injustice, falsehood, untruth'), formed with the negative prefix не- and правда ('truth, justice', derived from правый 'right, true, straight', Proto-Slavic *pravьda).

неправильно.etymology: Adverb formed with the negative prefix не- from правильно ('correctly, rightly'), derived from правильный ('correct, right') and правило ('rule'), ultimately from правый ('straight, right', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

неправый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic неправыи ('unjust, crooked, wrong'), formed with the negative prefix не- and правый ('right, straight, just', from Proto-Slavic *pravъ). In modern Russian, it is used almost exclusively in the short predicate forms **неправ / неправа / неправы** ('wrong, mistaken': ты неправ 'you are wrong').

нервничать.etymology: Formed in 19th-century Russian with the colloquial behavioral verb suffix -ничать from нервный ('nervous'), itself derived from нерв ('nerve'), borrowed via German Nerv / French nerf from Latin nervus ('sinew, tendon, nerve').

history.meaning: nervous → to act nervously, fret, worry

morphemes.meaning: to behave in a certain manner

нечего.etymology: Negative predicative pronoun (stressed on the first syllable: **не́чего**, literally 'there is nothing [to do]') inherited from Old East Slavic нечего, contracted from *не есть чего ('there is not of what', where не is fused with the lost present copula *е / есть and чего is the genitive of что 'what', Proto-Slavic *čьto). Distinct in stress and meaning from **нечего́ / ничего́** ('nothing').

history.meaning: there is nothing (to); no point in (+ infinitive)

нечего.notes: Followed by an infinitive (with an optional dative subject): **Мне не́чего сказать** ('I have nothing to say'), **Не́чего делать** ('There's nothing to do').

нигде.etymology: Negative locative adverb inherited from Old East Slavic никъдѣ, formed from the negative prefix ни- and где ('where', Old East Slavic къдѣ, from Proto-Slavic *kъde).

никак.etymology: Negative adverb formed from the negative prefix ни- and как ('how', from Old East Slavic како, Proto-Slavic *kako).

history.meaning: in no way, by no means, not at all

никуда.etymology: Negative directional adverb formed from the negative prefix ни- and куда ('where to, whither', from Old East Slavic кудѣ / куда, Proto-Slavic *kǫdě).
никуда.notes: Russian distinguishes location (**нигде** 'nowhere, in no place') from direction of motion (**никуда** 'to nowhere': *я никуда не пойду*).

ниша.etymology: Borrowed as an architectural term from French niche ('wall recess'), from Old French nichier 'to make a nest', going back to Latin nidus 'nest' (distant Indo-European cousin of Russian гнездо and English nest).

новый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic новъ, from Proto-Slavic *novъ, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos ('new'), cognate with English new, German neu, French neuf/nouveau, Latin novus, and Ancient Greek νέος.

нож.etymology: Нож is an inherited Slavic word, recorded as ножь in Old Russian and Old Church Slavonic. Vasmer connects its historical root with заноза, вонзить and пронзить: words involving a splinter, piercing or thrusting into something. That connection gives the knife word a history associated with a pointed or piercing object.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: нож

номер.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (via German Nummer or Dutch nummer) from Latin numerus / Italian numero ('number'). In 19th-century Russian inns and hotels, номер ('a numbered room') became the standard everyday word for a hotel room.

ночь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ночь (Old Church Slavonic нощь), from Proto-Slavic *noktь, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts ('night'), cognate with English night, German Nacht, French nuit, Latin nox, and Lithuanian naktìs.

ну-ка.etymology: Colloquial hortatory particle formed from the interjection/particle ну ('well, come on', inherited from Proto-Slavic *nu, cognate with English now and Latin nunc) + the enclitic particle -ка (shortened from тка / тако, used with imperatives to soften or urge an immediate action).

history.meaning: come on, let's see, go on

обидеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic обидѣти ('to wrong, injure, offend'), from Proto-Slavic *obiděti, reduced by haplology/dissimilation from *ob-viděti ('to look past, overlook, slight', from *ob- 'around, past' + *viděti 'to see', Russian видеть). From 'looking past someone with disregard', the meaning developed into 'to wrong, hurt, offend'.

history.meaning: to look past, slight → to wrong, offend

обидеться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed by adding -ся to обидеть ('to offend, hurt'), inherited from Old East Slavic обидѣти, from Proto-Slavic *obiděti (reduced from *ob-viděti 'to look past, slight').

обижать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of обидеть ('to offend, hurt, wrong'), continuing Old East Slavic обижати (with East Slavic ж from Proto-Slavic *dj; compare Church Slavonic обиждати), formed from *ob- ('around, past') + *viděti ('to see', Russian видеть). Originally *ob-viděti meant 'to look past someone, overlook, slight, treat with disregard', which developed into 'to wrong, offend, hurt'.

history.meaning: to overlook, slight → to wrong, offend

обижаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive verb formed from обижать ('to offend, hurt'), continuing Old East Slavic обижати, from Proto-Slavic *obiděti / *obidjati (reduced from *ob-viděti 'to look past, slight').

обложка.etymology: Formed in Russian from обложить ('to lay around, wrap, cover') + -ка: literally the protective outer wrap laid around the pages of a book or notebook.

обман.etymology: Deverbal noun from обмануть ('to deceive, cheat'), formed from the prefix об- ('around') and the Proto-Slavic root *man- ('to beckon, lure, delude', as in манить 'to lure, entice' and Lithuanian monai 'delusion, sorcery').

обмануть.etymology: Formed with the prefix об- ('around') on the Proto-Slavic root *maniti ('to beckon, lure, delude, trick'; compare манить 'to beckon, entice' and Lithuanian monai 'witchcraft, delusion'). The consonant cluster -бм- simplified from *об-мануть, literally 'to lure around, delude with false appearances'.

обманщик.etymology: Agent noun formed in Russian with the suffix -щик from обман ('deceit, trickery') / обмануть ('to deceive, cheat', built on the Proto-Slavic root *man- 'to lure, delude').

обманывать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of обмануть ('to deceive, cheat'), formed with the imperfectivizing suffix -ыва- on the stem обман- (from об- 'around' + Proto-Slavic *maniti 'to lure, delude, trick').

обнять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic обьяти / обняти ('to embrace, clasp around'), formed from the prefix об- ('around') and яти ('to take, grasp', Proto-Slavic *obъjęti, with epenthetic -н- generalized from nasal prefixes into the infinitive обнять and present обниму, while the past tense обнял preserves the older nasal-free stem).

оборудование.etymology: Verbal noun formed from оборудовать ('to equip, fit out with tools and machinery'), built with the prefix об- on the archaic noun орудие / орудъ ('tool, instrument, implement, affair', from Proto-Slavic *orǫdьje 'tool, business, gear'; compare Polish orędzie and Old High German arunti 'errand').

history.meaning: to fit out with tools → equipment, machinery

обстоятельство.etymology: Coined in the 18th century (featured in Trediakovsky and Lomonosov, on the model of Old Church Slavonic обстояние) as a structural calque of Latin circumstantia / French circonstance ('that which stands around an event: a circumstance'), formed from об- ('around', Latin circum-) + стоять ('to stand', Latin stāre) + -тельство.

обсуждать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обсѫждати (imperfective of обсѫдити / обсудить 'to judge from all sides, deliberate upon, discuss'), showing the Old Church Slavonic reflex -жд- for Proto-Slavic *dj (compare native East Slavic осужать), formed from об- ('around, from all sides') + судить ('to judge', from суд 'judgment, court', Proto-Slavic *sǫdъ).

общаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive/reciprocal verb formed from общать (Old Church Slavonic обьщати 'to make common, share, associate with'), derived from общий ('common, shared', from Proto-Slavic *obьťь, built on *ob 'around'). Literally, 'to share company or conversation with others'.

history.meaning: to communicate, talk with, socialize, hang out

общий.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обьщь ('common, shared, general'), where -щ- is the South Slavic reflex of Proto-Slavic *tj (compare native East Slavic вобче / вообще). Derived from Proto-Slavic *obьťь ('around, shared by those around'), formed from the preposition/prefix *ob ('around, about').

обязанный.etymology: Adjectival passive participle of обязать ('to bind around; to oblige, place under a duty'), borrowed in its Old Church Slavonic prefixal form об-язати (where East Slavic had обвязать), from *ob- ('around') + *vęzati ('to tie, bind', Russian вязать). Literally, 'bound by obligation' (paralleling Latin obligātus from ligāre 'to bind').

огромный.etymology: Derived from the Slavic root гром- ('thunder', as in гром 'thunder' and громить 'to smash, crash'). Originally meaning 'thunderous, stunning, awe-inspiring in scale' (compare Polish ogromny 'huge, vast'), the meaning shifted from auditory force to visual and physical immensity.

одежда.etymology: Borrowed in its Old Church Slavonic form одежда ('clothing, garment, attire'), showing the South Slavic reflex -жд- for Proto-Slavic *dj (compare native East Slavic одёжа), from Proto-Slavic *odedja, derived from *oděti ('to clothe, wrap around', Russian одеть), formed from *o(b)- ('around') + *děti ('to put, place', PIE *dʰeh₁-).

morphemes.meaning: put, clothe (Church Slavonic stem of одеть)

rootFamily.gloss: to put on (an item of clothing)

оказаться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed from оказать ('to show, render'), built from the prefix о- and казать ('to show, appear', Old East Slavic казати, Proto-Slavic *kazati). With the reflexive suffix -ся, оказаться literally means 'to show oneself to be', whence 'to turn out to be' or 'to find oneself in a place'.

history.meaning: to turn out to be; to find oneself (somewhere)

окно.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic окно, from Proto-Slavic *okъno, derived from *oko ('eye', from PIE *h₃ekʷ-). Like English window (from Old Norse vindauga, 'wind-eye'), Slavic named a window as the 'eye' of a house wall.

он.etymology: An inherited Slavic pronoun, recorded in Old Russian and Old Church Slavonic as онъ. Its older demonstrative sense connects “he” with “that one”; Vasmer compares other Slavic forms and Lithuanian anas, meaning that one or he.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: он

он.notes: Many simple prepositions require an initial н- in the third-person oblique forms: у него, к нему, с ним, о нём. Check the construction rather than adding н- after every preposition.

она.etymology: Она belongs to the inherited Slavic demonstrative-pronoun family also seen in он and оно. Vasmer records the feminine form она in Old Russian and Old Church Slavonic and compares feminine forms in the other Slavic languages. The older connection with pointing to that person survives behind its everyday meaning she.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: он (including она)

опаздывать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of опоздать ('to be late, arrive late'), formed with root vowel lengthening (о > а) and the imperfective suffix -ыва- from поздно / поздний ('late', Old East Slavic поздо, Proto-Slavic *pozdъ).

history.meaning: to be running late, be late (imperfective)

опасный.etymology: Derived from опасаться ('to beware, be on one's guard, fear') and archaic опасъ ('caution, guard, protection'), built from о- ('around') + пасти ('to herd, guard, watch over', from Proto-Slavic *pasti, PIE *peh₂- 'to protect, tend'). Originally опасный meant 'watchful, cautious, circumspect'; by the 18th century it shifted from the person exercising caution to the situation requiring caution ('fraught with danger, dangerous').

rootFamily.gloss: thank you (from спаси Бог, same root пас-)

операция.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via Polish operacja or German Operation from Latin operātiō ('work, performance, activity'), derived from operārī ('to work, labor') and opus ('work').

опытный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from опыт ('experience, experiment, trial'), a deverbal noun from опытать ('to test, try out, assay'), built from о- + пытать ('to test, inquire, probe', from Proto-Slavic *pytati). Literally, 'tested by trial, possessing practical experience'.

особенный.etymology: Extended adjectival form of особый ('special, separate, particular'), formed with the suffix -енный from особа / особь ('individual, person apart'), which goes back to the Old East Slavic prepositional phrase о собѣ ('by oneself, apart, separately', from о + собѣ, the dative/locative of the reflexive pronoun себя 'oneself').

особый.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic особыи ('separate, distinct, special'), formed from the archaic adverb особь ('apart, separately'), which originated from the Old East Slavic prepositional phrase о собѣ ('by oneself', where собѣ is the older East Slavic dative/locative of the reflexive pronoun себя 'oneself', Proto-Slavic *o sobě; compare Polish osobny 'separate').

ответить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic отъвѣтити, from Proto-Slavic *otъvětiti ('to answer, reply'), formed from the prefix *otъ- ('back, in return') and *větiti ('to speak solemnly, counsel, address', from *větъ 'counsel, pact', preserved in совет 'advice, council' and привет 'greeting').

ответственность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from ответственный ('responsible, accountable, answerable'), derived from ответ ('answer, reply; account', from ответить 'to answer', Proto-Slavic *otъvětъ). Coined in the late 18th century (recorded from 1789 by Karamzin) as a semantic calque of French responsabilité and German Verantwortung ('being answerable for').

отдавать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of отдать ('to give back, return, hand over'), formed from the prefix от- ('away, back') and давать ('to give', iterative of дать, from Proto-Slavic *davati, PIE *deh₃- 'to give').

history.meaning: to hand over, give back, return

отец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic отьць (and Old Church Slavonic отьць, vocative отче), from Proto-Slavic *otьcь ('father'), formed with the affectionate/diminutive suffix *-ьcь from *otъ ('father'), from Proto-Indo-European nursery word *átta ('daddy, father'; compare Ancient Greek ἄττα, Latin atta, Gothic atta, and Hittite attas).

отключить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix от- ('off, away, disconnecting') and ключить (built on ключ 'key, switch', from Proto-Slavic *kľučь 'hook, key, bolt'), on the model of включить ('to switch on') and выключить ('to switch off'). Means 'to disconnect, cut off (power, water, or a phone), switch off'.

history.meaning: to disconnect, cut off, switch off

отношение.etymology: Verbal noun formed from относить / отнести ('to carry away; to refer, relate') and относиться ('to relate to, treat'), a compound of от- ('from, away') + носить ('to carry'). In the 18th century it calqued French relation and German Verhältnis ('relation, attitude; in plural, interpersonal relationships').

отомстить.etymology: Perfective counterpart of мстить ('to take vengeance, avenge'), inherited from Old East Slavic отъмьстити, formed from the prefix от- / ото- ('back, in return') and мьстити ('to avenge'), a denominative verb from мьсть / месть ('vengeance, retribution'), from Proto-Slavic *mьstь (originally 'recompense, exchange, return payment', cognate with Sanskrit mithás 'mutually, alternately' and Gothic maipms 'gift').

history.meaning: retribution, payback → to pay back, avenge
to take revenge, get back at (+ dat.)

отпустить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic отъпустити ('to let go, release, remit'), formed from the prefix от- ('away, off') and пустить ('to let go, allow, release', from Proto-Slavic *pustiti, originally 'to make empty/free', from *pustъ 'empty, free', Russian пустой).

отравиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed from отравить ('to poison'), built from о- + травить ('to poison; originally to graze cattle on grass, consume with herbs/potions'), a denominative verb from трава ('grass, herb, medicinal or poisonous plant', inherited from Old East Slavic трава, Proto-Slavic *trava, from *truti 'to consume, wear away').

history.meaning: grass, herb → to feed on herbs / treat with herbal poison
to get poisoned, suffer food poisoning

отрезать.etymology: Formed from the prefix от- ('off, away') and резать ('to cut, slice', from Old East Slavic рѣзати, Proto-Slavic *rězati). Stress distinguishes aspect: perfective **отре́зать** ('to cut off, slice off') vs. imperfective **отреза́ть**.

официант.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century via German Offiziant or Polish oficjant ('subordinate official, functionary, attendant') from Medieval Latin officiāns (genitive officiantis), present participle of officiāre ('to perform a duty or service'), from Latin officium ('service, duty, office'). In Russian, the word narrowed from a minor civil or church attendant to a restaurant waiter.

очкарик.etymology: Colloquial expressive noun formed in 20th-century Russian with the compound suffix -арик (on the pattern of words like сухарик, комарик) from очки ('glasses, spectacles'), itself the plural diminutive of archaic око ('eye', Old East Slavic око, Proto-Slavic *oko, PIE *h₃ekʷ-).

очки.etymology: Plural of очко, the diminutive of archaic Russian око ('eye', from Proto-Slavic *oko, PIE *h₃ekʷ-). Attested from the 16th–17th centuries in the plural sense 'little eyepieces, spectacles'.

парень.etymology: Attested in Russian from the 17th century. Most etymologists (following Sobolevsky and Vasmer) derive парень from dialectal парь ('lad') or directly from Old East Slavic паробокъ / паробьць ('servant lad, youth', compare Polish parobek and Ukrainian парубок), formed with the archaic prefix па- and робъ ('servant, child, worker') and reshaped with the suffix -ень.
парень.notes: In modern colloquial Russian, парень means both 'guy, lad' and 'boyfriend' (мой парень). Its plural is irregular in everyday speech: **ребята** (or **парни**).

пасха.etymology: Borrowed in the Old East Slavic period via Old Church Slavonic пасха from Byzantine Greek πάσχα (páskha, 'Passover; Easter'), from Aramaic פַּסְחָא (pasḥā) and Biblical Hebrew פֶּסַח (pésaḥ, 'Passover', from pāsaḥ 'to pass over, spare'). In Russian, Пасха denotes both the Christian holiday of Easter and the traditional pyramid-shaped sweetened quark/curd cheese dish prepared for Easter.

паштет.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from German Pastete ('pâté, meat pie, pastry'), from Medieval Latin pastāta / Old Italian pastata, derived from Late Latin pasta ('dough, paste'), from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá, 'barley porridge, salted mess of food').

history.meaning: dough, paste → dish baked in pastry

пекарня.etymology: Built in Russian from пекарь 'baker' + the place suffix -ня, from the Slavic verb печь 'to bake, roast'.
пекарня.notes: Genitive plural inserts a fleeting е: пекарен.

передумать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix пере- (indicating redoing or altering a previous state) and думать ('to think', from Old East Slavic думати, Proto-Slavic *dumati). Literally, 'to think over again in a different way', i.e., 'to change one's mind'.

переехать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix пере- ('across, from one place to another') and ехать ('to go by vehicle, travel', from Old East Slavic ѣхати, Proto-Slavic *ěxati). Means 'to cross by vehicle, run over' or 'to move to a new home, apartment, or city'.

history.meaning: to ride across, move to another place

morphemes.meaning: across, from one place to another

перестать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic перестати ('to stop, cease'), formed from the prefix пере- ('across, over, through') and стать ('to stand, come to a halt', from Proto-Slavic *stati).

history.meaning: to come to a stop, cease

перец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic перьць ('pepper'), formed with the Slavic noun suffix *-ьcь from early Slavic *pьpьrь, borrowed via Latin piper or Byzantine Greek πέπερι (péperi) ultimately from Sanskrit पिप्पली (pippalī, 'long pepper').

history.meaning: pepper (spice or bell/chili pepper); (slang) guy, fellow

перила.etymology: Plural-only derivative built on the Slavic root of переть / опереться ('to press, lean, support oneself') with the instrument suffix -ило: literally 'the bars one leans on for support' along stairs or a bridge.
перила.notes: Always plural in modern standard Russian: держаться за перила ('to hold on to the railing').

песок.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пѣсъкъ and Proto-Slavic *pěsъkъ 'sand', related to Indo-European words for crushed grit and dust (compare Sanskrit pamsu 'crumbling soil, sand').
песок.notes: Drops the fleeting vowel -о- in all oblique forms: песок -> песка, на песке.

петрушка.etymology: Borrowed via Polish pietruszka (adapted from Czech petrzel and Middle High German petersilje), ultimately from Latin petroselinum and Ancient Greek petroselinon, literally 'rock celery' (petra 'rock' + selinon 'celery'). Reshaped in Russian to match familiar -ушка nouns.

печать.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pečatь, originally meaning a heated branding iron used to stamp livestock or wax, derived from the same root as печь 'to bake, burn, scorch'. From 'brand, seal' it expanded to 'printing press' and 'print'.

печь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic печь, where both the feminine noun печь ('oven, masonry stove', from Proto-Slavic *pektь) and the verb печь ('to bake', from *pekti) continue Proto-Indo-European *pekʷ- ('to cook, bake', cognate with Latin coquō).

пианино.etymology: Borrowed from Italian pianino, a diminutive of piano with the suffix -ino, so literally 'a little piano'. Russian uses it for the upright piano found in homes; the grand piano is рояль. Like other borrowed nouns in -о, it never changes its ending.
пианино.notes: Indeclinable: играть на пианино, у пианино, с пианино.

пиво.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пиво ('drink, beverage; beer, ale'), from Proto-Slavic *pivo, formed from *piti ('to drink', Russian пить) with the neuter noun suffix *-vo. Originally meaning any 'drink, potion', across most Slavic languages *pivo specialized to mean 'beer'.

пиджак.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from English pea jacket (originally a sailor's heavy short coat, itself from Dutch pijjekker 'coat of coarse wool'). In Russian the word shifted to mean an ordinary suit jacket or blazer.

пирог.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пирогъ, from Proto-Slavic *pirogъ, formed from *pirъ ('feast, banquet', itself derived from пить 'to drink'). Originally пирог named special festive stuffed bread baked for guests at a celebration.

писатель.etymology: Agent noun formed with the suffix -тель from писать ('to write', originally 'to paint, decorate with marks', from Old East Slavic писати, Proto-Slavic *pьsati, from PIE *peys- / *pik- 'to carve, mark, paint').

письмо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic письмо, from Proto-Slavic *pisьmo ('writing, inscription, letter'), derived from писать (*pьsati, originally 'to paint, trace designs, write', cognate with Latin pingō 'to paint').

пить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пити, from Proto-Slavic *piti ('to drink'), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃(i)- ('to drink'; compare Ancient Greek πίνω, Sanskrit píbati, and Latin bibō / pōtus).

rootFamily.gloss: to drink up; to have a drink

платить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic платити ('to pay'), from Proto-Slavic *platiti, a denominative verb built on *platъ ('piece of cloth, linen'). In early medieval Slavic trade, standardized pieces of woven linen cloth served as a medium of exchange and currency (compare Czech platit 'to pay' and plátno 'linen').

history.meaning: piece of linen cloth (used as currency) → to pay

плевать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пльвати (present плюю), from Proto-Slavic *pľьvati ('to spit'), an ancient onomatopoeic Indo-European verb (*spjew- / *pjew-; compare Lithuanian spiáuti, Latin spuō, Gothic speiwan, and English spew). In colloquial Russian, мне плевать (на что-то) means 'I couldn't care less, I don't give a spit about it'.

плохо.etymology: Deadjectival adverb formed from плохой ('bad'), originally the neuter short form of the adjective. Inherited from Old East Slavic плохъ ('simple, poor, weak, bad'), from Proto-Slavic *ploxъ, whose deeper Indo-European connections remain uncertain (Vasmer compares possible links to words for 'timid, startled' or 'flat, bare').
плохо.notes: Used both as a manner adverb (он плохо готовит) and as an impersonal predicate with a dative experiencer (мне плохо 'I feel unwell').

плыть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плыти (present плыву, older плову), from Proto-Slavic *plyti / *pluti ('to float, swim, sail'), from Proto-Indo-European *plew- ('to flow, float, swim'; compare Ancient Greek πλέω 'to sail', Sanskrit plávate 'floats, swims', Latin pluere 'to rain', and English flow / float).

history.meaning: to swim, float, sail (in one direction)

по-моему.etymology: Parenthetical adverbial phrase formed from the preposition по ('according to, in the manner of') + моему, the dative singular masculine/neuter of мой ('my, mine', Old East Slavic мои, Proto-Slavic *mojь), with ellipsis of мнению ('according to my opinion').

history.meaning: according to my (opinion) → in my opinion; my way

победа.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic побѣда ('victory, conquest'), a deverbal noun from побѣдити / победить ('to vanquish, overcome, defeat'), built on бѣда ('distress, compulsion, calamity', Russian беда, Proto-Slavic *běda). Originally 'the overcoming or subjugation of an adversary by force'.

победить.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic побѣдити ('to conquer, vanquish, defeat'), formed from по- and бѣдити ('to compel, force, overcome'), a denominative verb from бѣда ('calamity, distress, compulsion', modern Russian беда, from Proto-Slavic *běda 'necessity, distress', cognate with Gothic baidjan 'to compel' and Latin fīdō).
победить.notes: Famous in Russian grammar for lacking a standard 1st-person singular future form (*побежу / *победю are avoided in standard speech in favor of **я одержу победу** or **я смогу победить**).

повезти.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the inceptive prefix по- and везти ('to convey, carry by vehicle, pull a cart or sleigh', inherited from Old East Slavic везти, Proto-Slavic *vezti, from PIE *weǵʰ- 'to convey in a vehicle', cognate with Latin vehō and English wagon / way). From the image of a horse or fortune 'pulling one's cart smoothly along', the impersonal dative construction мне повезло ('it carried me well') became the standard Russian expression for 'I got lucky'.

history.meaning: to take by vehicle; (impersonal + dat. повезло) to be lucky

rootFamily.gloss: to carry by vehicle; to be lucky (impf.)

повод.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic поводъ ('rein, bridle, lead-rope; guidance, cause'), a deverbal noun from поводить / повести ('to lead along', built from по- + водить / вести 'to lead', Proto-Slavic *povodъ). From the literal 'bridle rein' by which a horse is led (still used in на поводу у кого-то), the word developed the figurative meaning 'that which leads to an action: a pretext, occasion, or reason'.

подарить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix по- and дарить ('to give as a gift, bestow'), a denominative verb from дар ('gift'), inherited from Old East Slavic даръ and Proto-Slavic *darъ ('gift', from the PIE root *deh₃- 'to give', as in дать 'to give' and Greek δῶρον 'gift').

history.meaning: to bestow, grant as a gift

поддержка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with the suffix -ка from поддержать / поддерживать ('to hold up from underneath, support'), built from под- ('under') + держать ('to hold'). In the 18th–19th centuries it also absorbed the figurative sense of French soutenir / support ('moral, political, or financial backing').

подойти.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix под- / подо- ('under, up to, near') and идти ('to go, walk'), continuing Old East Slavic подъити and Proto-Slavic *podъjьti ('to approach, walk up to').

history.meaning: to walk under or up to
to approach, come up to; to suit

подоконник.etymology: Transparent Russian spatial compound built from под- ('under, at the base of') + окно ('window') + -ник: the sill or ledge set directly beneath the window frame.

подписка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with the suffix -ка from подписать ('to sign underneath, subscribe'), built from под- ('under') + писать ('to write', Proto-Slavic *pьsati). Like Latin subscriptiō ('writing underneath'), подписка means both a periodical 'subscription' and a 'signed legal undertaking' (most famously in подписка о невыезде 'a signed undertaking not to leave town while under investigation').

подушка.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic подушька (Proto-Slavic *podušьka, from *poduxa). Etymologists trace it to *duxъ 'breath, air' via the idea of something puffed up or stuffed with down, though popular tradition has long reinterpreted it as под ухо ('under the ear').

поезд.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic поѣздъ ('a riding out, wedding or princely cortege'), a deverbal noun from поехать / ездить ('to ride, travel'). In the 19th century it was adopted for a railway train, parallel to French train and German Zug.

поехать.etymology: Perfective verb formed by adding the inceptive prefix по- ('setting off, starting an action') to ехать ('to go by vehicle, ride'), inherited from Old East Slavic ѣхати, from Proto-Slavic *ěxati ('to ride, travel').

history.meaning: to go by vehicle, set off

пожалеть.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix по- and жалеть ('to feel sorry for, pity; to regret, spare'), derived from жаль ('pity, sorrow'), inherited from Old East Slavic жаль ('grief, sorrow, compassion; grave mound') and Proto-Slavic *žalь ('sharp pain, grief', cognate with Lithuanian gė́la 'sharp pain').

history.meaning: to take pity on; to regret

rootFamily.gloss: it's a pity; feel sorry for

пожалуй.etymology: Fossilized 2nd-person singular imperative (пожалуй 'be so gracious as to grant!') of пожаловать ('to grant, bestow favor, show mercy'), formed from по- + жаловать ('to favor, feel affection/pity for', from Proto-Slavic *žalovati, related to жаль). Just as пожалуй + ста ('be so kind, sir') fused into пожалуйста ('please'), bare пожалуй grammaticalized as a parenthetical discourse particle meaning 'if you please → I suppose, perhaps, probably'.

history.meaning: be so gracious as to grant!

пожалуйста.etymology: Formed by fusing older пожалуй (imperative of пожаловать, 'be so kind, grant a favour', related to жаловать) with the old deferential enclitic particle -ста. While the first half clearly asks for gracious favour, Vasmer notes that the exact origin of the particle -ста (linked variously to сударь or old forms of стать/быть) remains debated.
пожалуйста.notes: Covers 'please', 'you're welcome', and 'here you go' when handing something over.

позже.etymology: Comparative degree ('later') of поздний / поздно ('late'), formed from the stem позд- (Old East Slavic поздо / поздьнъ, Proto-Slavic *pozdъ, built on *po- 'after') with palatalization before the comparative suffix *-je.

познакомиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed with the prefix по- from знакомиться ('to get acquainted'), derived from знакомый ('familiar, acquainted'), originally a passive participle in -м- from Old East Slavic знакъ ('sign, mark') and знати / знать ('to know', from Proto-Slavic *znati, PIE *ǵneh₃-).

поймать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic поимати ('to take, seize, catch'), formed from the perfective prefix по- and имати ('to take, grasp, catch', from Proto-Slavic *jьmati, iterative of *jęti 'to take', with initial *jь- coalescing after the vowel of по- into пой-).

morphemes.meaning: take, seize (from Old East Slavic имати)

поймать.notes: Forms an aspectual pair with **ловить** (impf. 'to try to catch, be catching') / **поймать** (pf. 'to catch').

полезный.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic полѣзьнъ / пользьнъ ('beneficial, useful, profitable'), formed from польза ('benefit, use, advantage', Old East Slavic польга / Old Church Slavonic польза, from Proto-Slavic *polьga, built on *lьg- 'light, easy', as in лёгкий). Literally, 'bringing ease or benefit'.

полицай.etymology: Borrowed during World War II directly from the phonetic pronunciation of German Polizei ('police', [poliˈtsaɪ]), specifically designating a local auxiliary policeman serving in the German occupation forces on occupied Soviet territory (Hilfspolizei).

полиция.etymology: Borrowed under Peter the Great in the early 18th century via German Polizei (older Policey) and Polish policja from Late Latin polītīa ('civil administration, public order'), from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía, 'citizenship, government, administration of a polis'), from πόλις (pólis, 'city-state').

полотенце.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *poltьnьce, a diminutive in -це of полотно 'linen cloth' — originally 'a small piece of linen' for drying one's hands or face.
полотенце.notes: Genitive plural inserts a fleeting е: полотенец.

полотно.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *poltьno 'woven linen cloth', showing regular East Slavic pleophony (-оло- from *-ol- between consonants; compare the Church Slavonic doublet платно and Polish plotno).

history.meaning: linen fabric; painter's canvas; railway roadbed

получать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of получить ('to receive, get, obtain'), formed from the prefix по- and лучать / лучить ('to hit a mark, obtain by lot', from Proto-Slavic *lučiti; compare случай 'chance, occasion' and благополучный 'fortunate').

history.meaning: to hit the mark, come by lot

получаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive/intransitive verb formed from получать ('to receive, obtain', imperfective of получить). The root луч- goes back to Proto-Slavic *lučiti ('to hit the mark, happen upon, receive by lot or fortune'; compare случай 'case, chance' and благополучный 'prosperous'). With -ся, получаться means 'to turn out, work out, succeed'.

history.meaning: to hit a target, happen by lot
to turn out, work out, come out

помоложе.etymology: Attenuated comparative formed by adding the prefix по- ('a bit, somewhat') to моложе ('younger'), the comparative degree of молодой ('young', Old East Slavic молодыи, from Proto-Slavic *moldъ, comparative *moldje, with East Slavic ж from *dj).

помощь.etymology: Adopted with the Old Church Slavonic reflex -щ- (compare native East Slavic помочь in dialectal/idiomatic бог в помочь) from Old Church Slavonic помощь ('help, aid, assistance'), from Proto-Slavic *pomoťь, formed from *po- and *moťь ('power, might', from *moťi 'to be able', Russian мочь).

поработать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the delimitative prefix по- ('for a while, a bit') and работать ('to work', from работа 'work', Proto-Slavic *orbota).

history.meaning: to work for a while, do some work

порода.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from породить ('to give birth to, generate, breed'), built from the prefix по- and родить ('to give birth, bear', from род 'kin, lineage, birth', Proto-Slavic *rodъ). Denotes lineage, stock, animal breed, or geological rock formation.

history.meaning: to beget, breed → lineage, breed, species

портрет.etymology: Borrowed via German Porträt from French portrait ('likeness, portrait'), originally the past participle of Old French portraire 'to draw forth, depict', from Latin protrahere ('to draw out, bring to light').

посадить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic посадити, formed from the perfective prefix по- and садить ('to make sit, seat, plant'), the Proto-Slavic causative *saditi ('to cause to sit, set') built on the o-grade of *sěděti / *sěsti ('to sit', PIE *sod-éye-ti, exact cognate with English set).

history.meaning: to seat; to plant; to imprison

rootFamily.gloss: to sit; to be in prison

посидеть.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the delimitative prefix по- ('for a while, a bit') and сидеть ('to sit'), inherited from Old East Slavic сидѣти and Proto-Slavic *ěděti / *sěděti (from PIE *sed- 'to sit').

history.meaning: to sit for a while; to spend time together

посметь.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix по- and сметь ('to dare, venture'), inherited from Old East Slavic съмѣти (and Old Church Slavonic съмѣти), from Proto-Slavic *sъměti ('to dare').

постоянно.etymology: Adverb formed from постоянный ('constant, permanent, steady'), derived from постоять ('to stand firm, abide'), built from по- + стоять ('to stand', from Proto-Slavic *stojati; compare Latin cōnstāns 'standing firm, constant').

постоять.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the delimitative prefix по- ('for a while') and стоять ('to stand'), inherited from Old East Slavic постояти, from Proto-Slavic *postojati (from PIE *stā- / *steh₂- 'to stand'). With за + accusative (постоять за себя), it means 'to stand up for, defend'.

history.meaning: to stand for a while; to defend
to stand for a while; to stand up for

построить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix по- and строить ('to build, construct; to arrange'), inherited from Old East Slavic строити ('to arrange, order, prepare, build'), from Proto-Slavic *strojiti, causative/denominative from *strojь ('order, arrangement, structure').

поступить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic поступити ('to step forward, proceed, act'), formed from the prefix по- and ступить ('to step, tread', from Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti). From 'stepping forward', it developed both the sense 'to act, behave' (поступить правильно) and 'to enter, enroll in an institution' (поступить в университет).

history.meaning: to act, behave; to enroll, enter

rootFamily.gloss: to step on; to arrive (of time)

похоже.etymology: Neuter short form and adverb of похожий ('similar, resembling'), derived from походить ('to take after, resemble', from по- + ходить 'to walk, go'). Used both as a predicate ('it looks like, it is similar') and as a parenthetical discourse marker ('it seems, apparently').

history.meaning: similar → alike; it seems, looks like

похожий.etymology: Derived from походить ('to resemble, take after, go along someone's path'), built from the prefix по- ('along, after') and ходить ('to walk, go', Proto-Slavic *xoditi), with the alternation д > ж before the adjectival suffix -ий. Literally, 'walking in the same way, taking after'.

history.meaning: taking after in gait/manner → similar, resembling

поцеловать.etymology: Perfective counterpart of целовать ('to kiss'), formed with the prefix по- from Old East Slavic цѣловати ('to greet, wish good health; to kiss'), derived from цѣлъ / целый ('whole, hale, healthy', Proto-Slavic *cělъ).

history.meaning: whole, hale → to wish health in greeting, kiss

появиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed with the prefix по- from явиться ('to appear, show oneself'), derived from явить ('to show, manifest'), from Old East Slavic явити and Proto-Slavic *javiti ('to make visible, reveal', from *javъ 'awake, manifest, open', as in наяву 'in waking life', cognate with Sanskrit āvíṣ 'openly, before the eyes').

history.meaning: manifest, visible → to show oneself, appear

правильно.etymology: Adverb formed from правильный ('correct, right, proper'), derived from правило ('rule, straightedge, rudder'), itself built with the instrument suffix -ло on правый ('straight, right, just', from Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

правильный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from правило ('rule, straightedge, guide'), derived from правый ('straight, right, just', from Proto-Slavic *pravъ). Literally, 'conforming to the rule or straight line'.

право.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic право ('right, justice, law'), substantivized neuter singular of правыи / правый ('straight, right, just, true'), from Proto-Slavic *pravъ ('straight, right'). Parallels the semantic development of German Recht and French droit ('straight → right, law').

праздник.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic праздьникъ 'feast day, holiday', derived from праздьнъ ('unoccupied, free from everyday labour', from Proto-Slavic *porzdьnъ): a day set free from ordinary work for celebration.
праздник.notes: The middle consonant -д- is silent in everyday pronunciation (pronounced [празник], spelled праздник).

предатель.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдатель ('betrayer, traitor, Judas'), formed with the agent suffix -тель from прѣдати / предать ('to hand over, deliver up to an enemy, betray'), a compound of прѣ- ('over, across') + дати ('to give', Russian дать; compare Latin trāditor 'traitor' from trāns-dare 'to hand over').

предлагать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдълагати ('to lay before, set forth, offer'), formed from the Church Slavonic prefix прѣдъ- ('before, in front of', East Slavic перед-) and -лагати (iterative of ложити 'to lay, place'). Literally, 'to lay something before someone' (an exact structural parallel to Latin prōpōnere 'to propose').

предложение.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъложение ('setting forth, presentation, offering'), the verbal noun of прѣдъложити / предложить ('to lay before, offer, propose'). In the 18th century, Russian grammarians (such as Lomonosov) also used it to calque Latin prōpositiō ('grammatical clause/sentence, logical proposition').

предупредить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдоупрѣдити ('to go ahead of, forestall, anticipate'), formed from прѣдъ- ('before') + оу- + прѣдити ('to go in front', from предъ / перед 'in front', Proto-Slavic *perdъ). In the 18th century, influenced by French prévenir ('to go before → to forewarn, notify in advance'), it acquired the modern meaning 'to warn'.

history.meaning: to forestall → to warn, notify in advance

предупреждать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of предупредить ('to warn, notify in advance; to prevent'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдоупрѣждати (showing the Church Slavonic reflex -жд- for Proto-Slavic *dj), built on предъ / перед ('before, in front').

history.meaning: to warn, notify in advance; to forestall

президент.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century, initially for heads of state colleges and academies, later for heads of republic states) via German Präsident and French président from Latin praesidēns (genitive praesidentis, 'presiding officer, governor'), present participle of praesidēre ('to sit before, preside over, guard', from prae- 'before' + sedēre 'to sit').

history.meaning: to sit in front / preside → presiding head

прекратить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣкратити ('to cut short, abridge, terminate'), formed from the prefix прѣ- (East Slavic пере-) and кратити ('to shorten', from кратъкъ 'short', East Slavic короткий, from Proto-Slavic *kortъkъ). Literally, прекратить means 'to cut short'.

history.meaning: to cut short, bring to an end

придумать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix при- (indicating addition or mental attainment) and думать ('to think'), from Old East Slavic думати and Proto-Slavic *dumati (from *duma 'thought, counsel', an early borrowing from Gothic dōms 'judgment').

признаться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed from признать ('to recognize, acknowledge'), built from the prefix при- and знать ('to know', from Proto-Slavic *znati, PIE *ǵneh₃-). With the reflexive suffix -ся, признаться means 'to acknowledge about oneself, confess, admit' (often in love: признаться в любви).

прийтись.etymology: Perfective reflexive/impersonal verb formed by adding -сь to прийти ('to come, arrive on foot', from при- + идти, Proto-Slavic *prijьti). From the concrete sense of two parts 'coming together into alignment, fitting' (прийтись по вкусу 'to suit one's taste'), the impersonal dative construction мне пришлось + infinitive developed the sense 'it fell to my lot to, I had to'.

history.meaning: to come to fit, fall to someone's lot
to fit; (impersonal + dat.) to have to

rootFamily.gloss: to have to (impf.); to be related to

принимать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of принять ('to take, accept, receive'), inherited from Old East Slavic приимати, formed from the prefix при- ('to, towards') and -нимать (with epenthetic н- reanalyzed from prefixes ending in a nasal, from Old East Slavic имати 'to take', iterative of яти, Proto-Slavic *jьmati).

history.meaning: to receive, accept, take (medicine, guests, a shower, or a decision)

приставка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with the suffix -ка from приставить ('to set against, attach, place beside'), built from при- ('to, beside') + ставить ('to put, set upright', from Proto-Slavic *staviti). In the 18th century Russian grammarians used приставка to calque Latin praefixum ('prefix'); in the late 20th century (from телеприставка / игровая приставка, an electronic unit attached to a TV set), it became the everyday word for a video game console or set-top box.

проводить.etymology: Formed from the prefix про- ('through, along') and водить ('to lead, conduct', iterative of вести, from Proto-Slavic *voditi). Represents two homographic verbs in Russian: (1) perfective проводить (paired with провожать), meaning 'to escort, see off, accompany to the door or station', and (2) imperfective проводить (paired with провести), meaning 'to conduct, spend (time), or carry out'.

history.meaning: to see off, escort (pf.); to spend time, conduct (impf.)

программа.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century via French programme or German Programm from Late Latin programma ('public notice, edict'), from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma, 'public written notice, agenda'), from προγράφω (prográphō, 'to write beforehand or in public', from προ- 'before, forth' + γράφω 'to write').

продолжать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of продолжить ('to lengthen, prolong, continue'), formed from the prefix про- and должить ('to make long'), derived from долгий ('long', Old East Slavic дългыи, Proto-Slavic *dъlgъ, cognate with English long and Latin indulgeo). Literally, 'to draw out in length, prolong'.

проект.etymology: Borrowed under Peter the Great (early 18th century, often spelled прожект from French before settling on проект after German Projekt) from Latin prōiectum ('something thrown forth, plan, design'), neuter past participle of prōicere ('to throw forward, stretch out', from prō- 'forth' + iacere 'to throw').

проиграть.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix про- (in the sense of loss, forfeiture, or spending through an action) and играть ('to play'), from Old East Slavic играти and Proto-Slavic *jьgrati.

history.meaning: to lose (in a game, bet, or contest)

произойти.etymology: Perfective counterpart of происходить ('to happen, occur; to originate from'), formed from про- ('forth, through') + из- / изо- ('out of') + йти / идти ('to go', Proto-Slavic *iti). Literally, 'to come forth out of', whence 'to come to pass, happen, occur'.

history.meaning: to come forth, issue → to happen, take place

происходить.etymology: Imperfective verb borrowed from or modeled on Old Church Slavonic происходити ('to go forth, issue from, originate'), formed from про- ('forth, through') + ис- / из- ('out of') + ходити ('to go, walk'). From 'coming forth, originating', it developed the modern meaning 'to happen, take place'.

history.meaning: to happen, occur; to originate from

проследить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix про- ('through, thoroughly') and следить ('to track, watch, keep an eye on'), derived from след ('footprint, track', from Proto-Slavic *slědъ).

history.meaning: to track down; to see to it, make sure

просыпаться.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of проснуться ('to wake up'), formed from the prefix про- ('through, out of') and the iterative stem -сыпать (with lengthened zero-grade vowel ы < *ū from the root of спать 'to sleep', Old East Slavic съпати, Proto-Slavic *sъpati, from PIE *swep- 'to sleep').
